the following is an extract from the report by mr cláudio monteiro de aguiar on the eu strategy for sustainable tourism [2020/2038 (ini) ] (a9-0033/2021).
the rapporteur. - madam president, the tourism and travel industry is facing the worst, the most dramatic period in its history. the losses faced by tourism businesses and their employees today are 11 times higher than those recorded during the economic crisis of 2009. the sector, which is one of the most resilient and has been the engine of growth in countries, needs the union's solidarity and support more than ever. the european parliament in this report presents a set of clear answers for the tourism and travel industry and also for transport, which can and should be implemented. we've been asking for coordination since the beginning of the pandemic crisis. we have presented solutions for implementing a european test protocol, starting with european investment and also with government investment, at no cost to european citizens. the tourism sector needs short-term liquidity to help avoid the scourge of insolvency and thus save jobs and people's lives, as well as capitalisation and the strengthening of equity to secure its future. recovery is expected to be difficult and long. the recovery plans of each of the 27 must therefore include projects for tourism. without this support, there will be no green and digital transition. the criteria for the award of financial support should be based on the sector's contribution to the gross domestic product of each country and region. countries such as portugal and the outermost regions of europe have their wealth heavily leveraged in the tourism sector and should therefore be the subject of increased attention. the union needs to do more, it needs to have more powers, and the european parliament is ready and is asking the commissioner for a strategy and an action plan. we need a marshall plan for the sector, as you said a short while ago, but we need it for tomorrow because if we leave things as they are, those who can capitalise on their businesses and those who cannot will be left behind with unpredictable social and economic consequences. the tourism and travel industry believes in european responses, in common responses, but for that, there needs to be political will. the union must come together, join forces and have the political courage to adopt a european policy for tourism, to accept that in the future it is possible to set up a european agency for tourism which will work with data, which will use big data to find the best solutions and which will support all stakeholders, but also all those who are directly or indirectly involved in this sector of activity, in making policy decisions. this period is crucial, this report is crucial to make it clear to our fellow citizens, the european citizens, that europe is coordinated, that europe has measures, that europe will prepare funding to support businesses, to support institutions, to support european citizens in this difficult phase in which the health crisis, this covid-19 pandemic crisis has struck the whole world, but in particular the weaker regions and with more delicate economies and this is, in fact, the moment for the european parliament to give a proof. this is a report with a clear path to sustainable tourism, to tourism of the future. let there be political courage in the union to defend transport, tourism and travel effectively. we will thus be able to live up to the expectations of our citizens.
member of the commission. – madam president, honourable members, allow me to congratulate ms monteiro de aguiar on her report and the constructive ideas for the future of european tourism. the commission shares your vision and goals for a sustainable, digital and resilient tourism ecosystem. the pandemic has deeply disrupted europe’s tourism ecosystem, weakening its immediate ability to invest and rebound. it has affected all regions of europe, and particularly harshly those heavily reliant on tourism, including coastal areas, islands and the eu’s outermost regions. at the same time, there is hope. europeans are eager to travel again. as the epidemiological situation remains worrisome, we need to put in place measures that protect public health and ensure safety but that also allow safe travel and tourism. we need to protect businesses and jobs in tourism and exploit the business potential of greening the sector. the eu has mobilised unprecedented emergency support for the tourism ecosystem and individual companies. we have also been working with member states to coordinate action as regards restrictions of free movement and safety measures. thanks to the eu vaccination strategy and efforts made across the eu, we can expect that member states will be gradually reopening to tourists in the coming months. to facilitate a safe reopening, the commission proposed last week a package of measures, including a legislative proposal for a digital green certificate. currently, member states have different conditions of entry, such as pcr tests and quarantine. we already have many problems in the recognition of test results from other member states. with the rollout of vaccinations, the worry is that member states propose diverse solutions on how to allow vaccinated citizens to enter their country and on how to prove that they are vaccinated. this could lead to a real barrier to free movement and to the functioning of the single market. hence the need for a european solution applied evenly by all countries. let me be clear: this certificate is non—discriminatory. it cannot and should not be used as a precondition for free movement, nor should it be used as a tool for border control. it will include proof that a person has been vaccinated or the results of tests and information on covid—19 recovery. with the summer travel season approaching, the certificate should be in place by mid—june at the latest. in parallel to the institutional negotiations, the member states and the commission are already working on the technical solution. the commission is counting on your support for its swift adoption. health and safety standards are key to reassure travellers and tourists. they also guarantee a level playing field for businesses. the commission has asked the european standardisation organisation to work on a standardisation product for all eu tourism businesses, with an easily recognisable visual identity. this should also be ready in time for the summer. regarding the long—term perspective, the commission is fully mobilised to help restart the tourism ecosystem with concrete actions. following the safe reopening package of last week, the commission will propose next month an updated industrial strategy. it will include measures to draw lessons from the crisis and strengthen the resilience of the single market economy and its 14 industrial ecosystems, including tourism. the commission is also working with member states and stakeholders to develop a european agenda for tourism with a shared long—term roadmap. among the priorities, we are considering sustainable destination and tourism services, including an eu ecolabel and emas tourist accommodation. the european year of rail is an excellent opportunity to boost sustainable ways of travelling and unlock new destinations when tourism can restart. we also need digitalisation and improved data sharing to allow for informed, safe travel spread across more destinations and, of course, the upskilling and reskilling of workers, including through the pact for skills in tourism. due to the pandemic, the investment needs of the tourism ecosystem are the highest among all the industrial ecosystems. in this context, the recovery and resilience facility, along with the new multiannual financial framework, will play a crucial role. we hope that member states and the tourism industry will seize these unprecedented opportunities. honourable members of parliament, protecting businesses and jobs will be at the heart of the eu’s agenda, as will our commitment to help rebuild resilient and sustainable tourism. i am confident that together we can relaunch a stronger tourism ecosystem and maintain the european union as the world’s leading destination.

in writing. the covid-19 pandemic, which has been raging in europe for over a year, has taken a heavy toll on the tourism industry. in recent months, due to the second and third waves of the pandemic, most operators in this sector have again been forced to reduce or completely suspend their activities. therefore, without adequate and immediate financial support from the european union and its member states, micro, small and medium-sized enterprises in particular will not survive the current crisis. the commission will continue to monitor the implementation of the union's macro-financial assistance to the countries of central and eastern europe, including the countries of the former soviet union, and to monitor the implementation of the union's macro-financial assistance to the countries of central and eastern europe. the commission considers that the aid is compatible with the internal market within the meaning of article 107 (3) (c) of the treaty. the covid-19 pandemic has also highlighted the urgent need for a european tourism policy. the inclusion of tourism in the eu's shared competences, the creation of a separate budget line for tourism in the eu's multiannual budget and the establishment of a european tourism agency are all actions needed to maintain europe's position as the world's most popular tourist destination and tourism as the third largest sector of socioeconomic activity in the community.
in writing. cohesion policy is the european union's largest and most important investment tool. it can therefore potentially play a key role in combating climate change and make a significant contribution to the objectives and targets of the european green deal. but let us not forget that climate policy and the associated energy transition have a very strong and inseparable socio-economic dimension. the pursuit of climate neutrality in the european union requires many member states and their citizens to make concessions and sacrifices that they may not be prepared to make. the path to a green deal must be fair, leaving no one behind, otherwise cohesion policy will only serve to deepen the differences between countries and regions in europe. in my view, this report goes far beyond interinstitutional and political agreements, promoting actions that may harm the citizens of the union. the report called for a complete and almost immediate phase-out of fossil fuels, including natural gas. this is contrary to the fundamental right of member states to decide on their own 'energy basket'. member states can achieve climate neutrality only within their capabilities and in their own individual way.

madam president, it is regrettable that judicial cooperation in civil matters was not part of the eu—uk future partnership negotiations and the trade and cooperation agreement (tca). this lack of cooperation may have disastrous effects on european consumers and also on victims of human rights violations all around the world. the key here is the lugano convention, an international legal cooperation agreement. without this agreement in place, it will be very difficult for anyone to hold uk companies accountable. for both companies and consumers in the eu, this may mean that court decisions from the eu may not in practice be enforceable in the uk anymore. access to justice may require very expensive litigation in the uk. for victims of human rights violations, this may mean that they cannot rely on parent company liability in the uk as the uk courts may consider that another forum outside the uk is more appropriate to decide the case. once again, the victims may be stuck in court in a third country, in a litigation against a subsidiary or supplier, resulting in a court decision that may be impossible to enforce. the good thing, however, is that the uk does not want this to happen. the uk wants to rejoin the lugano convention and all other members of the convention support its membership. we need more legal cooperation, not less, and the eu must not block the uk’s accession.

the rapporteur. mr. chairman, please! ladies and gentlemen! as regards discharge for the agencies i have worked with, management solutions are often too complex or inadequate. for example, some agencies have too many boards, which threatens to make decision-making inefficient and increases administrative costs significantly. the agency's international reach is often limited. in most agencies, accountability and performance should be improved and reporting streamlined in view of the qualified opinion on the legality and regularity of payments underlying the accounts issued by the european court of auditors. i will now present the findings concerning two agencies: the european asylum support office and the agency for the cooperation of energy regulators. starting with easo: the court of auditors found that it had obtained sufficient assurance that the office's annual accounts were reliable and sufficient audit evidence as to the legality and regularity of the revenue underlying the accounts. however, the court has issued qualified opinions on its findings notified for the financial years 2016, 2017 and 2018 on the legality of the regularity of payments. for the financial year 2019, the court found other errors relating to payments, with the exception of the consequences of errors in 2016, 2017 and 2018 and payments relating to observations for 2019. the payments underlying the annual accounts for the year ended 31 december 2019 are legal and regular in all other material respects. it should be noted that the new executive director was appointed on 16 june 2019. as regards the european anti-fraud office's investigation, following the receipt of the olaf report at the end of 2018, the office initiated three disciplinary proceedings which are currently ongoing. the procurement procedures of the office with regard to temporary staff in greece and the premises rented by the office in lesbos were irregular. the office's tender procedures for temporary staff in italy were irregular, although payments had not yet been made under these contracts. the office's procedures for selecting and contracting external experts consistently lacked a robust audit trail, which in turn resulted in a lack of evidence that the office treated experts equally in its selection procedures. i'll now move on to the other agency, acer. let's start with budget and financial management. the budget implementation rate was 99,50%, which was above the agency's planned target of 95%. the commission shall be assisted by the european parliament and the council. however, the court has delivered a qualified opinion on the legality and regularity of the underlying payments, the total amount of which was incorrectly paid corresponds to eur 988 138, representing 6,3% of all payments made by the agency in 2019. irregular payments were found in relation to two irregular procurement procedures which were not carried out in accordance with the tendering procedures. in addition, recruitment procedures were not properly applied in the selection process, resulting in the agency not respecting the principle of equal treatment and not applying effective internal controls. however, the agency reported that its internal control framework is effective, its annual assessment of its implementation did not reveal any deficiencies and the agency's strategic audit plan for 2017-2019 was fully implemented. the agency shall also take further steps to increase the transparency of its activities, such as reporting on meetings of agency staff with external parties (in particular meetings of the agency director with organisations and self-employed persons) and publishing them on the agency's website. at the same time, we should insist that the agency report to the discharge authority without delay on the development of the ongoing activities in the field of it management and market surveillance of remi (i.e. the regulation of the european parliament and of the council on wholesale energy market integrity and transparency). we're waiting for that information. finally, i would like to thank all those who have helped to prepare these discharge reports. i thank the european court of auditors for their cooperation, and in particular my colleagues, and i address these words of special thanks to mrs kamila wrzesińska.
the commission has also proposed that the council adopt a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, (the microphone was switched on late) [...] of the libe opinion i will focus on the gai agencies which also played a key role in 2019, supporting european institutions and member states in increasingly challenging challenges in the protection of fundamental rights, security, judicial and police cooperation in criminal matters and migration. in carrying out their tasks, the gai agencies as a whole respected the principles of sound financial management and obtained positive assessments on the reliability of the accounts, the legality and regularity of the operations by the court of auditors, with the only partial exception of easo, which nevertheless took the necessary measures to remedy the previous difficulties. in 2019, the court of auditors again notes that the agencies have committed to follow up on the observations of previous years, although there remains room for improvement, for example in procurement procedures. the recommendation to grant discharge for 2019 to all gai agencies, with the exception of frontex, is therefore consistent, and it is therefore necessary that the investigations initiated, including by olaf, provide full clarity on any critical issues identified.

rapporteur for the opinion of the committee on women’s rights and gender equality. – madam president, good afternoon from poland. it is a good opportunity to assess the extent to which the principle of gender mainstreaming has been integrated within the eu’s policies. unfortunately, we haven’t achieved the progress that we hoped for. we still lack an effective methodology allowing to track gender-equality spending. we also still don’t have an independent budget line for measures specifically targeting gender equality, including gender—based violence. we also should remember that gender equality still hasn’t been mainstreamed across the union budget to the same extent as other policies, as stressed by the european court of auditors. so, it is clear, we must increase our efforts here. at a time when women are on the front line of the covid—19 crisis, whilst their rights are under attack in certain states, gender mainstreaming should not only be a concern of the committee on women’s rights and gender equality (femm) and other dgs, it should be a priority for all of eu institutions and agencies. unfortunately, this is still not the case.
on behalf of the ecr group. - madam president! - i have to go. i'm not going to let you get away with this. the european globalisation adjustment fund has always been a symbol of solidarity and i am convinced, and i hope, that it will remain so in the years to come. it's a fund that's designed to help us tackle some of the most important challenges in an increasingly globalized world, and that's why it's good that it includes the ones that are most important to workers and to the community: the socioeconomic transformation, the transition to a low-carbon economy, the digital transformation, automation, brexit. i'm glad we're all agreed on the fundamental change, which is to lower the threshold for granting support from 500 to 200 employees. the fund offers a wide range of support for different groups of employees in large enterprises, in small and medium-sized enterprises and for the self-employed. in the face of the challenges i have already mentioned, the ability to reach as many people as possible with support is undoubtedly one of the greatest advantages of this fund, and i hope that member states will be able to take advantage of this. financial assistance from the fund may be used for a variety of activities to support workers, including personalised training or retraining, job search assistance or self-employment assistance. this is very important, especially at this time when we are dealing with the covid-19 crisis and i think that today, when millions of citizens in europe are dealing with the consequences of this pandemic, such support from the european globalisation adjustment fund is very important and necessary. we all hope that this pandemic, this crisis, will end very quickly, that there will be sufficient vaccine supplies, and that everyone will be able to function safely.
i'm not going to let you get away with this. ladies and gentlemen! the european globalisation adjustment fund does not change its character, it remains interventionist. its main purpose is to provide support to workers affected by mass redundancies. it has also become more general. the fund finances active labour market instruments, it is a support fund. the aid is still one-off and limited in time. he certainly needed to be changed, and the changes we make improve his efficiency. the fund becomes more available, better used. the most important and valuable change is the reduction of the dismissal threshold to 200. this is a better solution than the one that was proposed 10 years ago. the same applies to the increase in funding for the selfemployed, which is capped at eur 22 000 per beneficiary. the change to smes in one region now affects many different sectors of the economy, rather than one sector as before. one of the reasons for the insufficient use of the fund so far has been the slow and bureaucratic procedure, which is extremely time-consuming and also requires a huge administrative effort. simplifying procedures is also an important and good change. we should adopt and complete this legislative procedure quickly.

the next item is the debate on the recommendation for second reading by the committee on legal affairs and the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs on the council's position at first reading with a view to the adoption of a regulation of the european parliament and of the council establishing the 'justice' programme and repealing regulation (eu) no 1382/2013 [06834/1/2020 - c9-0138/2021 - 2018/0208 (cod) ] (rapporteurs: heidi hautala, katarina barley) (a9-0146/2021).
rapporteur. – mr president, on 30 may 2018, three years ago, the european commission submitted a proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council to establish the justice programme. now, a little less than three years later, we are in a position to adopt the final text. here in the european parliament, preparing this justice programme was a joint effort of the committee on legal affairs (juri) and the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs (libe). i had the honour and pleasure to be the rapporteur on behalf of juri. the cooperation with the libe rapporteur has always been excellent. i started with mr weidenholzer and i continued with ms barley. i also want to thank the parliament services, especially the juri and libe committees, for their relentless work that, in my view, led to excellent results with the help of the commission. the negotiations with the council and the commission were tough but fair. in the end, we reached an outcome that is not just technical, but mirrors the eu’s values and seeks solutions to concrete problems we are facing. the rule of law and fundamental rights in the eu cannot be defended without a well-functioning, independent and impartial justice system. the programme focuses on persons and entities which contribute to make our common values – equality, rights and rich diversity – alive and vibrant. it is important that all relevant stakeholders, including civil society actors, are involved in the development of the legal system and can access funding. in this case, the justice programme has eur 305 million in total under this programme. it’s just one fifth of the citizens, equality, rights and values programme, but it is essential to guarantee a uniform european sphere of law. this programme has three main objectives: it facilitates and supports judicial cooperation in civil and criminal matters, promoting the rule of law, independence and impartiality of the judiciary; it supports and promotes judicial training, with a view to fostering a common legal, judicial and rule of law culture; and it facilitates effective and non-discriminatory access to justice for all, and an effective redress, including by electronic, e-justice means. special attention is given to mainstreaming. in the implementation of all of its actions, the programme shall seek to promote gender equality, the rights of the child and child-friendly justice, the protection of victims and the effective application of the principle of equal rights and non-discrimination. while judicial cooperation may not necessarily be in the forefront of the eu’s climate action, parliament secured that this programme ought also to support activities that respect the climate and environmental standards and priorities of the union and the ‘do no harm’ principle of the european green deal. the programme foresees different kinds of actions that are eligible for funding. the programme can be used, for example, for awareness-raising, mutual learning and the exchange of good practices among stakeholders to improve knowledge of union policies and union law. it can also be used for analytical and monitoring activities to improve knowledge and understanding of potential obstacles to the smooth functioning of a european area of justice. it can be used to train relevant stakeholders, and let me mention here that we have new emerging areas of law because our society is evolving in terms of technology and social systems and the like and we have newly emerging areas, for instance environmental justice, which the justice professionals have to understand better. the programme will also be used for developing and maintaining information and communication technology (ict) as well as e-justice tools, which will take into account privacy and data protection. this is a long list, but what makes me particularly happy is to see how the programme clearly acknowledges the role of civil society in this field too. the promotion of the rule of law will benefit from specific support and the commission will report annually on the performance of the programme and the use of the funds for each specific objective, including actions linked to the promotion of gender equality. the interinstitutional negotiations were concluded on 18 december 2020. in february 2021, both coreper, as well as the juri and libe committees in this parliament, accepted the outcome of the negotiations. as a final step, the council adopted its position on 19 april 2021. i can confirm that its position fully reflects the agreement reached and that in the council, all delegations, except for hungary and poland, voted in favour. as the co-rapporteur, i cannot but hope that the regulation is swiftly adopted and enters into force as soon as possible.
member of the commission. – mr president, after the conclusion of a successful trilogue in december last year, i am pleased to talk to you again today about the justice programme. the commission welcomes the agreement reached between the co-legislators on this important programme. this agreement shows that there is a strong determination by the eu institutions to support the further development of a european area of justice. let me once again thank the european parliament for its strong support concerning this file, and notably the rapporteurs, ms hautala and ms barley. the justice programme will support major political actions. to mention a few: the roadmap for a comprehensive european rule of law report, with an eu-wide scope and objective annual reporting; the new judicial training strategy aimed at equipping judges, prosecutors and other justice professionals for the challenges of the 21st century, such as artificial intelligence; and the eu strategy on victims’ rights, focused on empowering victims to report crimes and get the support they need. le programme «justice» soutiendra également la création de systèmes judiciaires plus efficaces et facilitera l’accès des citoyens à la justice par des moyens numériques, ce qui revêt une importance particulière dans le contexte de la crise de la covid—19. il est en effet devenu évident que les citoyens et les entreprises doivent avoir accès à la justice, également en ligne. je vous remercie à nouveau de votre soutien continu eu égard à ce programme et je me réjouis bien entendu de prendre connaissance de vos observations.
on behalf of the ppe group. mr president, colleagues, i would like to thank the rapporteurs and commissioner reynders for their constructive work on the dossier. the european union has achieved a great deal by building a common area of justice, but we live in a time of serious global challenges that undoubtedly require all member states to do more in the name of the rule of law, an independent judiciary, mutual recognition and trust. it is therefore important to have a well-functioning european area of justice, with maximum ease of access to the judicial system in cross-border legal situations and with active judicial cooperation in civil and criminal matters. the adoption of the new justice programme is of paramount importance in this regard. with our support, we will confirm our commitment to see this important instrument for the protection of justice, rights and values of the european union put into practice as soon as possible. we know that good cooperation is based on mutual trust. this includes providing support for training and exchange of magistrates, as well as for the development of independent, transparent and efficient national justice systems. the appropriations will be used for activities that protect and strengthen fundamental values such as human rights, the rule of law, freedom, democracy and equality. it is now increasingly important, in the context of the justice programme, to promote the effective application of union legal instruments and to develop e-justice. in modern practice, more active use of electronic means makes it possible to improve the efficiency of judicial proceedings and to increase access to justice for citizens and businesses.
the commission is therefore proposing to amend the proposal to the effect that the commission should be able to take part in the discussions. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your work. i would like to begin by thanking the two rapporteurs for the european parliament, heidi hautala and katarina barley, for their work on this very important programme. i believe that we as members of parliament have reached a really good compromise with the council, which ensures that we continue to live in an open, democratic, pluralistic and inclusive society. what's this justice program all about? it is the very heart of european cooperation. european cooperation can only work if we trust each other, and that requires the core of the rule of law to work in all member states. that is the justice system, that is the good work of judges. where there are attacks on civil society, where judges and prosecutors are intimidated, we must respond as a community. we need to work together to make sure that our justice system is protected, and the justice program is a good answer to that. but is that all? i'm not going to. for example, there are strategic lawsuits against civil society organizations, there are strategic lawsuits against journalists -- so-called slapps -- there are strategic lawsuits against public participation, and frankly, this cannot continue. that is why the justice programme is just another building block in our fight for more justice and the rule of law in the european union.

on behalf of the id group. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, the justice programme for 2021-2027 is officially pursuing commendable objectives. with a budget of €305 million, it aims to promote the independence of the judiciary in each member state and to promote access to justice for all, without discrimination of any kind. such objectives can only be agreed. unfortunately, he also pursues more subtle but more formidable goals. it therefore advocates raising awareness of national judges about eu policies, under the pretext of better training. this is tantamount to confusing the obviously necessary legal training of judges with their submission to the union's ideological propaganda, which must be firmly rejected. finally, the justice programme is used to provide massive subsidies to associations and ngos that contribute to the respect of the rule of law, but under the cover of this kind presentation, it is actually a matter of financing george soros' galaxy of associations which, under the pretext of promoting an open society, constantly fight the sovereignty and identity of european nations. i personally cannot accept that and for these reasons i shall vote against the justice programme and the report which praises it.

rapporteur. – madam president, we live in difficult times. the terrorist threat to our community is still present and it is our responsibility to keep citizens safe and to prevent terrorist attacks. however, in order to do so, it is necessary to understand the terrorists’ modus operandi and its evolution. as an example, i will use the long—standing statement of umar patek, the organiser of terrorist attacks on bali in which more than 200 people were killed. he said, during his trial, for those who do not know how to commit jihad, they should understand that there are several ways to know jihad. this is not the stone age. this is the internet age. we have facebook, we have twitter. as he said, this is what happened. the internet has become the most important safe haven and tool for terrorists today. on the internet, terrorists recruit by spreading propaganda, including among children and young people. they provide attacks and violence from the internet, spreading propaganda to youngsters and children. there they show their attack, call for attack and spread a radical agenda. as a continuation, let me show some examples. in 2020, facebook removed 43.4 million pieces of content of a terrorist nature or containing incitement to attack. in the previous year, it was 25.5 million pieces of content, so as you can see, it is a significant increase with the advent of pandemics and people being locked in their homes. in 2019, twitter reported that it blocked more than 300 000 accounts linked to a terrorist organisation or used to spread terrorist propaganda both linked to radical islam and to left- and right-wing extremes. in 2016, it was 100 000 accounts, so one can see an upward trend. today, terrorist groups have their own media, magazines, editors. the internet and modern technology have allowed terrorist groups to post content that they fully control. a staff of specialists from such terrorist groups prepares professional information and propaganda campaigns, documentaries and magazines published online. they’ve directed executions. that is why our response was needed. the regulation will allow member state to immediately remove terrorist content. it has introduced, among others, the principle of one hour, which means that the most dangerous content will be removed as soon as possible after publication. for example, member states finally received a working tool to stop live broadcasting from a terrorist attack or mass shooting. this is a groundbreaking project and the first in the history of the eu that implements such a powerful tool in cross-border cooperation between member states in this area. one country will have the right to send a removal order to another country. the order will apply to everyone in the eu, including those outside the eu. failure to comply with the order will result in large financial penalties. the new regulation will help to counter the spread of extremist ideology online. the regulation will ensure that what is illegal offline is illegal online. removal orders can be sent by any member state to any online platform established within the eu. however, according to the compromise reached, the authorities of the member states where the content host is located will have 72 hours to analyse and possibly challenge the withdrawal order if it sees, for example, a clear violation of freedom of expression. in addition, we are carrying a new framework for the cooperation between public institutions and the private sector. we will all now have a duty to act in solidarity to tackle terrorism. this regulation will ensure that the online platforms play a more active role in detecting terrorist content online and that such content is removed within a maximum of one hour. at the same time, potential threats to freedom have been removed. there will be no mandatory filtering of the internet. new safeguards for freedom of speech, freedom of press and media, as well as freedom for legal content, for instance, journalists’ research, artists, educational content, too. moreover, it safeguards content which represents an expression of polemics or controversial views in the course of public debate. it was a very difficult project. thanks to the involvement of parliament’s excellent negotiation team, whom i would like to thank, it was possible to reach a compromise. i would also like to thank the commissioner and the council. i strongly believe that the terrorist content (tc) regulation is a good and balanced text which balances security and the freedom of speech and expression on the internet, protecting legal content and access to information for every citizen in the eu. it is a new tool based on mutual cooperation and trust between states fighting together in the one cause against terrorists. the europe union today has gained a powerful new tool to fight terrorists, and this is very good information for our community.

in writing. 2020 has been a very difficult year for europe. the pandemic has killed thousands and caused economic collapse in many countries. despite the lockdown and restrictions, the terrorist activity has not been contained. there have been several attacks, including in france and austria. islamic terrorists are still active in europe. isis cells and al-qaeda-linked organizations such as the syrian hts are pouring their propaganda online, radicalizing the youth. i am glad that the union has taken action on this matter. today we are debating a new tool that offers new possibilities for the fight against radicalism, a tool based on european community, trust and support. the cross-border order to remove radical content and terrorist propaganda is finally coming into force. it's a symbol of mutual trust between nations, as opposed to the threat that affects us all, regardless of national borders. i look forward to the next solution similar to those adopted today, for cross-border evidence collection in electronic crimes.
in writing. when terrorism threatens our security, our rights and freedoms, it is important to adopt appropriate clear, coherent and harmonised tools to remove terrorist content from the internet, to prevent the use of the internet to disseminate terrorist content. however, it is necessary to ensure the security of online services while guaranteeing full respect for fundamental rights, i.e. freedom of expression and the acquisition and dissemination of information. the adopted text defines what constitutes terrorist content online, provides for legal remedies in case of blocking or removal of content and prevents social media platforms from becoming censors. the new rules require the authority responsible for issuing removal orders for terrorist content, controlling cross-border orders from another member state, supervising measures implemented by a hosting provider to prevent the appearance of terrorist content on its services, and imposing sanctions for non-compliance with the obligations arising from the regulation. the model proposed in the regulation is based on cooperation between the competent state authorities and hosting service providers. the key obligation imposed on hosting service providers under the draft law is to remove or disable access to terrorist content within one hour of receiving an order from the competent authority. the second important solution is for hosting providers to take measures to prevent the dissemination of such content.

in writing. today's debate concerns the regulation establishing the european defence fund (edf), the record of which is the result of years of work and a compromise reached in interinstitutional negotiations (including between member state governments in the eu council). poland has actively participated in its preparation and supports the content of the regulation as agreed between member states and in the trilogue with parliament and the commission. the fund will primarily fund joint research and development in defence equipment and technologies and capacity building in multinational projects of eu priority. the fund will provide an alternative, cost-effective and risk-minimising mechanism for the procurement of military equipment through european military-technical cooperation. it is also the first time in eu history that the eu's common budget has supported defence-related research and development. it is important that eu-based companies can count on the support and development of new technologies in the important defence sector. the edf is a key component of the eu's defence policy and is the main instrument for the implementation of the eu's defence policy.

madam president, i am glad that we can talk about industrial strategy today, because industry not only creates 35 million jobs in the european union, but it is at the heart of our economic functioning and is a key area for our european economic recovery. today, we know that it is not only affected by the pandemic situation, but also by the rapid development of digitalization and our ambitious environmental goals. but i am sure that we have a chance to come out of this crisis empowered and industry can play this key role if we highlight three aspects. firstly, it is the common market. secondly, the role of small businesses and thirdly, the development of human resources. as regards the common market, we must complete it, particularly in the area of services, and not only implement the service directive, as the commission rightly proposes, but also implement and liberalise all services and have a level playing field for the digital common market as well. in the area of small businesses, we need to fundamentally improve access to capital, i.e. complete the capital union. we need to break down the barriers, the bureaucracy. what an important role the position of sme envoy will play. and last but not least, we must ensure that quality human resources are supported. this concerns not only entrepreneurship education in schools, but also the extension of the erasmus plus programmes, erasmus for young entrepreneurs. i am confident that if we put emphasis on these aspects, then industry will play a successful role in economic recovery.
madam president, ladies and gentlemen, we have seen during the pandemic that the main cause of economic drift in the european economic system has been our manufacturing industry. the best debt is debt for production. we must not forget, in times like these, of smart working and beyond, that there are factories where there are people working. to protect our manufacturing we must, as the industrial strategy rightly says, protect our strategic autonomy. what does that mean? it means taking action in certain areas, as has been said by my colleagues. in the steel industry, so-called green steel should not be penalized, so we cannot afford to export such large quantities of scrap, the most important recyclable raw material for our industrial systems. the same was said for semiconductors: the digital transition is not possible if europe produces only 9% of the world's semiconductors, compared to about 50% 20 years ago. and finally, the health issue has introduced into the industrial debate a great diatribe around patents: the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. patents should not be extended, they should be protected so that production is increasingly competitive.
i welcome the adoption of the revised industrial strategy and analysis, which has confirmed the strong dependence of certain industrial sectors, such as the technology and pharmaceutical sectors, on suppliers from outside the european union. and while the covid-19 pandemic has accelerated social transformation, it has also deepened already existing socioeconomic inequalities. it is the workers who have borne the brunt of this crisis. the revised industrial strategy therefore had to take greater account of the many labour market changes that have emerged from this crisis, such as remote work, while at the same time in many countries we are witnessing a worrying increase in the share of volatile and insecure forms of employment. the commission will continue to monitor the implementation of the union's energy strategy and its implementation in the member states, in particular through the implementation of the energy union strategy.
madam president, in light of the post-pandemic challenges, it is important to focus on how we can fortify our industry in an extremely competitive and inter-dependent environment in key strategic sectors, taking into account that we have to avoid further carbon leakage. in this regard, we have to work also towards diversifying in the national supply chain and pursuing in the national partnership to increase preparedness on a sector-by-sector basis. one of the sectors which is also mentioned in the commission’s strategy and where we have to invest heavily is batteries. batteries are the key component for the wider uptake, not only for immobility and renewables, but they are bound to become the catalyst to materialise the european green deal’s ambition, and that is to become climate neutral by 2050 and also to have companies become world leaders in clean products and technologies. we need more like the european battery innovation initiative: an important project of common interest that supports research and innovation in the battery value chain. to help member states – among them my home country, greece – it will provide up to 2.9 billion in funding in the coming years, and the public funding is expecting to unlock an additional nine billion in private investment: that is more than three times the public support. we need more projects like that. we need more europe investing for research and innovation in strategic sectors. we need to stop playing catch-up with our global strategic competitors. we have to join forces and lead the way.
madam president! while covid-19 has done a lot of damage, it has also taught us a valuable lesson about integration. we must draw lessons from it for the future of the european economy. first, the common market is the core of the european economy, but it is not yet as common as it could be. i would like to remind you of the enormous problems facing crossborder workers and entrepreneurs who have fallen victim to the chaotic reintroduction of national borders and regulations. the commission has therefore welcomed the proposal for an emergency single market instrument to ensure the free movement of persons, goods and services in the event of crises. it's time to send national egos back to the lamus. the second issue is that the post-pandemic recovery of the eu economy is a unique opportunity to achieve an industrial, green and sustainable transformation. the funds from the reconstruction fund or the fund for just transformation cannot feed into 19th century economic thinking. the future is self-government, economic freedom and innovation.

in writing. i am very pleased that in the european parliament we are increasingly able not only to discuss climate change but also to try to prevent it. climate change and continuous environmental degradation have a direct impact on freshwater resources, ecosystems and entire communities, and this in turn negatively affects the effective enjoyment of human rights, including the right to life, food security, safe drinking water and sanitation, health, housing, self-determination, work and development. increasingly, the effects of climate change are not only felt by the least developed countries, although they are the ones most affected, but also by the highly developed countries, including many european countries. the best example of this is the situation that took place in poland in skierniewice in 2019. the drought had caused the water to run out of the taps, and many smaller towns had to be supplied with water. such examples are growing year by year throughout europe. i therefore call on you to act effectively and swiftly to not only prevent further changes but above all to repair the damage that has already been done. it is very important that climate activists and indigenous peoples defending their territory receive adequate support and can count on justice when defending their territory and values.

member of the commission. – madam president, i’m happy to take part in this debate today relating to parliament’s interim report on amending the regulation establishing a european union agency for fundamental rights, known as ‘fra’. the commission’s proposal amending the fra founding regulation, tabled in june last year, was made in response to a request from this parliament and a number of member states. our proposal has two main objectives. the first is to clarify that following the entry into force of the lisbon treaty, the agency works within all the competences of the union – not of the former community. as a consequence, the agency also works in the area of the common foreign and security policy, the former so-called second pillar, and in the area of police and judicial cooperation in criminal matters, the former third pillar. the second objective of the proposal is to modernise the functioning and governance of the agency in line with a political commitment made in 2012 by parliament, the council and the commission to the so-called common approach for decentralised agencies. in the context of the envisaged modernisation of the fra regulation, we proposed removing the unnecessary multiannual framework procedure. this was also a request from parliament. as you know, this file has been blocked for half a year due to the veto of one member state. through discussions at ministerial level and other efforts, i can see that work has progressed well in the council, in particular on the inclusion of the former third pillar (police and judicial cooperation in criminal matters) in the fra remit and on the alignment of the fra regulation with the common approach for decentralised agencies, which will entail, in particular, the discontinuation of the multiannual framework procedure. this is very good news as it will enable the agency to work more independently and efficiently. our goal is now to converge all efforts and positive energies towards national recovery and resilience plans are a solidarity response by the european union to the impacts of the pandemic crisis. its funding model represents a step forward in the deepening of the european partnership and opens up the possibility of effective cooperation in the simultaneous realisation of the priorities of the member states and the strategic options of the union. diversity is an asset of the european union. the impact of the pandemic has not been felt in the same way in the different member states. response plans shall reflect the responses considered necessary in each specific context. in this context, and without prejudice to the absolute urgency in implementing the plans, the scrutiny of the european parliament, as an institution legitimised by the direct vote of citizens, in particular the scrutiny of the continuous evaluation by the european commission and the council, is an asset to ensure coherence and promote synergies that reinforce europe's commitments to the green deal, the green, democratic and inclusive digital transition, sustainable growth, territorial cohesion, convergence and the realisation of the pillar of social rights. consistency in the priorities and the necessary responses, without conditionality beyond those which shape the values and principles governing the union.

in writing. the european parliament's textual contribution to the 75th and 76th sessions of the united nations general assembly again does not address the essential issues of taking account of the work of the un to date or of addressing current and future global challenges. instead, the text was saturated with lessons and political appeals, repeated as a mantra by the left-liberal side of the parliament. one of these absurdities is that the text criticizes the sovereign choice of our country and poland to join a declaration of conservative values, just because it dares to go against the mainstream ideology of the eu. the recommendation contains passages imbued with political ideology, such as the call for a move to qualified majority voting in the council in the area of the union's common foreign policy. in addition to having nothing to do with the un general assembly, proposals to abolish unanimity are contrary to the eu's basic treaties and would deprive smaller member states of the opportunity to effectively promote their interests in shaping the union's common foreign policy. the text makes numerous references to the global compact on migration, which neither hungary nor several european member states supported, since its provisions can be interpreted as an invitation to illegal migrants. it is unacceptable that the left-liberal side has diverted another parliamentary report from its original purpose and filled it with its own political ambitions, calling into question the seriousness of the whole european parliament.
the next item is the recommendation for second reading from the committee on foreign affairs and the committee on development, on the council position at first reading with a view to the adoption of a regulation of the european parliament and of the council establishing the neighbourhood, development and international cooperation instrument – global europe, amending and repealing decision no 466/2014/eu of the european parliament and of the council and repealing regulation (eu) 2017/1601 of the european parliament and of the council and council regulation (ec, euratom) no 480/2009 (06879/1/2021 – c9—0191/2021 – 2018/0243(cod)) (rapporteurs: michael gahler, charles goerens, maria arena, rasa juknevičienė) (a9—0198/2021).
i have to say that i am not in favour of this. the commission has already made a number of proposals. i'm not going to let you get away with this. we are adopting today the eu regulation on the global europe programme. this regulation lays down the objectives, procedures and financial means of european foreign policy and our development cooperation. with the sum of all the important contents and rules and the resources of almost 80 billion euros, we are laying the foundations for the external action of the european union for the next seven years. certain rules also apply to cooperation with the candidate countries. the instrument therefore affects the use of almost eur 100 billion from the multiannual financial framework. we would like to see the european parliament's influence in this context strengthened to the point of genuine participation in the decision-making process on the national programmes. but unfortunately the council and the commission were not prepared to do so. the main task of the european commission therefore remains to make the selection decisions and to decide on the content of the country programmes. the commission is bound by the regulation to the political provisions of our international agreements, but also and especially to the political decisions and formal decisions of the council and parliament. in this way we are responding to the will of the european citizens who are calling for a strong and united foreign policy of the european union. as a parliament we will in future review more frequently and more closely the country programmes and concrete projects implementing the priorities of our foreign policy. i therefore welcome the newly established geopolitical dialogue with vice-president borrell and the commissioners responsible closely with them, setting european standards wherever possible. by sharing this part of the european way of life, we are rendering a valuable service to the improvement of living conditions in many countries. we help create security and prosperity. we are strengthening the bonds between our peoples and states. this will help our partners to resist the pressure exerted on them by russia or china, for example. europe is extending the zone of stability and freedom on and around our continent. with the global europe programme, we are making additional commitments and strengthening our commitment to climate, nature and the environment. we are doing more than we have done in the past to promote stability and traditional security as a prerequisite for development cooperation. and we are the rapporteur. madam president, madam commissioner, by signing the global europe document, we are bringing to an end three years of detailed analysis of a project to give europe more weight in the world. in keeping with its values, the union does not take the easy way out. by standing up for women, who are still too often oppressed, the european union is advocating the right to equality. by making the fight against poverty one of its highest priorities, the european union is siding with the weak. by devoting most of its resources to combating climate change, it is standing up for the right of future generations to live in decent conditions. by applying the principle of partnership in its relations with developing countries, the union deals with its partners on an equal footing. respecting the views of its partners, the union does not want to impose anything on them, either brutally or subtly. by signing a document that commits some €90 billion to its foreign policy for the next seven years, it gives predictability to its partners. by recommending that its member states participate in the union's efforts in the framework of so-called joint programming, it makes its external action more coherent and more effective. by merging ten instruments into one, the european union improves its responsiveness, reduces decision-making time and simplifies cooperation with its partners. by including the missions of the european development fund in the new instrument, the european union is putting an end to a contradiction. the contradiction was that democratic principles were being preached all over the world, while the european parliament was being denied the right to exercise its budgetary prerogatives in a vital area of foreign policy. the european parliament has been negotiating with the council for months and years. in addition to the more fundamental issues relating to development, cooperation with third countries, international law and security, the european parliament is keen to become more involved in the governance of the new instrument. he was helped by the great professionalism and example of the officials of the development and foreign affairs committees and the assistants of the correspondents. i would like to pay special tribute to them for having succeeded in clearing a path full of obstacles. their efforts, along with those of the colporteurs, were not in vain. parliament has now taken a step forward in the programming of an instrument by means of a delegated act negotiated at the last minute, without, however, replacing the commission, which remains the first responsible body for the policy choices to be made in the context of this instrument. today, and especially during the current pandemic, the time has come for the strategic state in our countries. the european union, with an instrument of approximately 90 billion, has the task of federating and sharing the resources it has with those of the member states, for the good of humanity. at a time when the savagery of external relations threatens to become the rule, the european union is trying to impose civilised relations between nations that respect each other. just because the bet is hard to win doesn't mean you shouldn't do it. humanity deserves better than blackmail, the status quo, exclusion, intimidation, threats of war, denial of human rights and the suppression of freedom of expression. dignity is not measured in millions of dollars. a day, a month, a year of peace remains difficult to evaluate financially. the conflict that could have been avoided is not visible. is this a handicap for the european union in its external relations? yeah, i guess i could. but what at first glance might be seen as a weakness in the face of global actors who ignore our values is in fact the nobility of our approach, better known from today on as 'global europe'.

on behalf of the ecr group. - madam president! - i have to go. the treaty of lisbon has changed the procedure for determining the provisions governing the exercise of investigative powers. article 226 of the treaty provides that the detailed rules for the exercise of the investigatory powers are to be laid down by the european parliament, acting by means of regulations on its own initiative in accordance with a special legislative procedure after obtaining the consent of the council and the commission. it is worth recalling that the council and the commission have pointed out that the essence of the parliament's powers of inquiry is that they are exercised by means of political rather than judicial accountability, and that the european parliament's supervisory function must be exercised within the generally accepted framework and functions conferred on it by the treaties. the right of the european parliament to exercise political control in the european union and to exercise its powers of inquiry in accordance with article 226 of the treaty should therefore be respected, but with due regard for the interinstitutional balance and the competences of the member states and the other institutions of the european union. the clue to the whole matter is contained in that last sentence, 'with due regard for the competence of the member states', the national states. the phenomenon of the european union, the phenomenon of the european parliament, as a member of the european parliament, as a european, as a pole, as a citizen, i am proud to sit in this house, but i cannot think of taking over the powers that the left of the chamber sometimes tries to impose on us. you talk a lot about democracy, about respecting the will of the voters. let me give you an example. the former prime minister of the polish government, today mep, mrs beata szydlo, received over half a million votes. what have you done? madam president, european citizens elect their meps. european citizens give us the task of representing them and require us to exercise our mandate in good faith and in their interests. european citizens place their trust in the european parliament and therefore have the right to have us look after the smooth running of the union and the proper spending of the money from the european union budget. the right of inquiry of the legislature against the executive is natural in absolutely any member state, is part of the principles of the rule of law and contributes to the fair separation of powers. the role of the european parliament's right of inquiry at eu level is the same, but the way it was established in 1995 no longer corresponds to european realities. it's inadequate and inefficient. in 2014, both the parliament and the council and the commission expressed their institutional and political will to have a new legal text in this regard. in 2019, after five years, this procedure was resumed. it's 2021. we're in the middle of a pandemic, and for the next few years, we have the largest cumulative budget ever put on the table by the european union. however, we are facing a deadlock as regards the european parliament's right of inquiry. we are talking about making european funds conditional on respect for the rule of law in the countries of the union. but what is happening in the european institutions? the council, the commission and the parliament must be examples of transparency, fully committed to european principles and values. therefore, an appropriate legal framework is needed for the full exercise of parliament's right of inquiry. it is the cornerstone of democracy and is based on the legitimacy given to parliamentarians by the vote of european citizens. on their behalf and in the letter and spirit of the union treaties, i call on the commission and the council to accept parliament's request for an effective inquiry mechanism as a matter of urgency. every piece of european legislation must be protected, and the right of inquiry ensures that we do that.
madam president, this is not just a theoretical debate. the lack of a clear legal framework for our right of inquiry has very concrete consequences. as chair of the parliament’s committee of inquiry on the protection of animals during transport, i have first-hand experience of this. the committee i chair does not want to blame other institutions; we want to help uncover current issues, to contribute to finding better solutions. but for us to be able to fulfil this mission, we rely on the full cooperation of all institutions. if an inquiry committee invites member states for an exchange of views, they should respond to the invitation. if an inquiry committee sends requests for information, we currently expect other institutions to cooperate, but can do little when they start disputing the parliament’s competences and hiding behind their legal service’s interpretation. instead of a battle between legal services, we need clear rules and procedures for the implementation of the right of inquiry. this is a crucial element of a parliamentary democracy.

member of the commission. – mr president, minister, honourable members, while in this house women’s representation has a better record – at 40% – compared to the eu average, men still outnumber women in positions of political power. on average, women account for just one in three of the seats in the eu’s national parliaments, and only 21% of leaders of major political parties are women. the increased use of social media and online tools in politics have provided great opportunities in terms of inclusion, participation in public debates and access to information. however, as we all know, there is also a downside to this development: the exposure to online violence, threats and harassment. last year, the world wide web foundation found that 52% of young women and girls had experienced online violence, including threats and sexual harassment. hateful online targeting makes it even more difficult to allow women to participate in public life. it can dissuade women from running as candidates in elections or from participating in public online debates, and can also lead to women ending their political careers prematurely. online attacks and disinformation are used to undermine women’s political credibility and question their decision—making capabilities. when violence occurs online, women are both the primary targets and are also forced to be the first responders. on social media platforms they are the ones who have to request the deletion of the hateful comments after they have been posted. a study by the inter—parliamentary union and the parliamentary assembly of the council of europe shows that 85.2% of the female parliamentarians interviewed had experienced psychological violence. almost half of the respondents reported having received death threats or threats acts, such as the killing of parliamentarian jo cox in 2016. in extreme cases, as shown by a unesco study on journalists, these attacks are accompanied by a rise in viral disinformation and through digital conspiracy networks. online violence can be part of an orchestrated campaign or can come from individuals sharing the same – often misogynist or racist – prejudices. in barring women from participating in public life and in spreading gender misinformation, these attacks are attacks on our fundamental values. democracy and freedom of expression are the main pillars of the pluralist societies the eu stands for. when women are not fully represented in positions of power, we are faced with a serious democratic deficit. online hate and violence can have a chilling effect on women’s participation in our democracies. we must ensure that women and groups who can be marginalised as victims of online violence are safe to raise their voices in public debates without fear of being attacked and discredited. the commission is strongly committed to ending online abuse in all of its forms. madam president! given the current legal situation on animal welfare and the level of agricultural development in the european union, the european parliament's resolution on the 'end the cage age' citizens' initiative is, in my view, unnecessary in the current situation. first, the claim that cages are the cause of suffering for a huge number of livestock is not supported by evidence, it is not applicable to the current situation in the european union agriculture. secondly, animals currently kept by farmers in the european union are kept in cages that comply with all animal welfare regulations. these animals do not suffer, but rather, the farmers reward them with high productivity and healthy production. third, the prohibition of inhuman treatment of animals has been established for years by welfare laws in the member states of the european union. fourth, a professional assessment of the scale of the problem is necessary. only after the results of the inspections, which the commission is due to present in 2023, can there be a serious discussion about animal welfare and the 'end the cage age' initiative.

in writing. fighting climate change is a shared responsibility for all of us to protect our world. the adoption of the eu climate regulation is an important step in this process. with the symbolic discussions over, it is time for responsible action, and three principles should be considered. the european commission and the european parliament must, above all, respect the principle of rationality. the legislative proposals that will be published in the near future should be based on a thorough analysis of the potential benefits and costs, supported by impact studies, and should be drawn up on the basis of reality, avoiding radicalism. it's important to stop the left's unrealistic ambitions to turn climate policy into a debate. the principle of sovereignty is also of paramount importance. climate action should be based on cooperation and agreements between member states and should not lead to a reduction in the competences of nation states. the related legislative proposals should take utmost account of the specificities of the member states. finally, without equity, there can be no successful green transition. the costs of climate action should therefore not be passed on to people, families and businesses through the price of food and energy needed to sustain life. keeping government costs low and keeping companies competitive is the main task of policy debates in the coming period.
the covid—19 pandemic has made it clear that the green and digital transition are not just an empty phrase championed in brussels, but the new reality for society and businesses all over our continent. as europeans call for more action to protect our planet and companies adjust to the new reality that climate change brings, our policy—making needs to keep up. the commission’s proposal for a european green deal and the 2030 climate target for reduction of net greenhouse gas emissions by at least 55% are welcome steps in this regard. the agreement that we are voting on during this mini—plenary session makes several positive and forward—looking steps: fixing the 2030 target for net 55%, making the 2050 climate—neutrality target a collective target on an eu level, the composition of a climate advisory board, non—binding sectorial roadmaps, climate partnerships and battery and hydrogen alliances. it is not enough to merely talk about the need for a sustainable future, we must outline how we plan to get there and then take concrete steps in that direction. the agreement on the european climate law is a positive development in bringing about a sustainable resilient future for our citizens.
in writing. i welcome the interinstitutional agreement on the climate law. the agreement strengthens the european framework for climate action by introducing, inter alia, the following elements: - an overall objective of achieving climate neutrality by 2050; - an ambitious 2030 climate target of at least a 55% reduction in net emissions compared to 1990, specifying the contribution of emission reductions and removals; - a commitment to negative emissions beyond 2050; - the establishment of a european scientific advisory committee on climate change, which will provide independent scientific advice; - stricter provisions on adaptation to climate change; - strong coherence between union policies and the objective of climate neutrality; - a commitment to initiate dialogue with various sectors to prepare sectoral roadmaps to chart the path to climate neutrality in different areas of the economy. i congratulate the rapporteur!

intergenerational bonds, including through the promotion of mentoring and volunteering, and the crucial importance of providing older people with adequate long-term health care and supporting initiatives based on the silver economy, mentoring and ways of activating older people. it should be the senior who decides whether he wants to work longer or whether he can devote himself to other social roles, such as caring for grandchildren or community service. we also call for action to improve the quality of life of our seniors, adapted to their needs in public spaces, housing, transport. the report therefore calls for the european union to encourage member states to make greater use of eu funds, such as the european social fund plus and the european regional development fund, to adapt infrastructure for older people. this includes safe and accessible urban transport, as well as public buildings and housing that are adapted to the needs of older people. i am very pleased that the report mentions the efforts to preserve traditional crafts, because we must not forget their invaluable contribution to the material heritage of our culture. it is the elderly who are now the kindergartens, which will promote the development of intergenerational bonds and combat the loneliness of older people, as intergenerational solidarity is one of the fundamental values of the european union. and i cannot imagine a prosperous europe without respect for the elderly. we also propose the establishment of a year of intergenerational solidarity and older people's activity. this is a reference to the initiative of 2012, when the european union first tried to tackle the problem of ageing populations. many of the tasks set out then remain relevant today, and the coronavirus pandemic phenomenon. many of you said that ageing is a challenge, but it is also an opportunity since we said at the beginning that in the last 50 years we live 10 years more, which means that we live longer and healthier lives, so this is also very important. and i have to highlight once again that this is the first ever commission which assigned one portfolio to demography, which shows how important demography is for us in europe. so your report shows that tackling ageing requires a whole-of-government approach. you identify a common goal of ensuring intergenerational solidarity and upholding the rights of everyone at all stages in life. i have been listening carefully to the points you raised. many principles of the european pillar of social rights relate to ageing, including the principle of lifelong learning, access to quality and affordable health and long-term care, pensions, many others. in synergy with the green paper, the european social rights action plan announced several initiatives relevant for ageing policies including the initiative on long-term care in 2022. the european union gender equality strategy is also relevant in tackling ageing trends. it delivers on the commission’s commitment to achieving a union of equality. women often align their decision to work and how to work with their caring responsibilities. they carry a disproportionate burden of unpaid work, which constitutes a significant share of economic activity. accumulated lifetime gender employment and pay gaps result in an even wider pension gap and consequently older women are more at risk of poverty than men. this is what many of you highlighted today. demographic change is happening in real time. never before have citizens enjoyed such long and healthy lives. this is a major achievement of our social market economy model. addressing demographic change is key to building a fairer and more resilient society. the european union and its member states can prevent or limit the negative impact of ageing. i reiterate once again, this is mostly in the competence of the member states. for this, we need the firm commitment and engagement of young and older people. we need to foster intergenerational solidarity and responsibility with enabling policies. i want to thank parliament for your work on ageing policies, and we look forward to continued cooperation on demography.
