in writing. poland supports the priorities of the incoming slovenian presidency on current challenges, in particular in the context of the recovery from the covid-19 pandemic and the complex international situation. we believe that working on resilience and preparing for possible future crises is crucial. from poland's perspective, work on the 'fit for 55' climate and energy package will be particularly important. in our view, the key elements of the package include: the revision of the ets; the objectives of the common effort to reduce (cer); the revision of the regulation on land use emissions and utilisation, land use change and forestry (lulucf). poland supports the initiative of the conference on the future of europe. we believe that the key to its success is the broadest and most direct participation of civil society. in addition, it should take into account the voice of key eu partners, and therefore the representatives of the western balkans as potential future eu members should be guaranteed to participate in the conference. poland supports the slovenian presidency's programme in the priority area of a credible and secure eu, capable of ensuring security and stability in its neighbourhood. we welcome the announcement of a focus on the eu enlargement process towards the western balkans, which will help to rebuild the eu's credibility in the region. we agree on the need to develop strategic cooperation with the us and nato, especially in the context of responding to common threats and challenges. we also offer our full support and assistance in the preparations for the eastern partnership summit in december this year.
in writing. hungary is one of the biggest supporters within the eu of the eu accession of serbia and other western balkan countries. we have long been disappointed to see some member states, mostly for reasons of internal politics, avoiding the subject of enlargement and blocking the acceleration of accession processes and the opening of new negotiating chapters, when the security of europe would require the acceleration of enlargement. over the years, successive eu presidencies have raised the issue of enlargement, but there seems to have been a lack of courage and political will to link the western balkans firmly and definitively to the eu. slovenia is an expert on the western balkans, and i therefore ask and encourage the slovenian presidency to do everything possible to achieve a common position with the member states sceptical about enlargement. this would be of particular importance for serbia as a key country in the region.
in writing. i very much welcomed the trio presidency declaration on ageing and the council conclusions adopted during the german and portuguese presidencies. i fully support the trio's position that demographic change is at least as significant as the challenges of climate change and digital transformation and should therefore be treated by the european union with equal commitment. we're at a critical juncture. the commission published a green paper on ageing and a european strategy on the rights of persons with disabilities. the un has declared 2021-2030 as the decade of healthy ageing. it is a very good moment to raise public awareness of the rights of older people, their contribution to economic and social life, the value of intergenerational learning and the importance of intergenerational solidarity. it is also time to turn declarations into concrete programmes and initiatives, both legislative and non-legislative. to meet the challenges of the pandemic, to make europe more resilient, to rebuild our economy, we need the strength, the wisdom, the talent of all generations. i will therefore be following closely the slovenian presidency's efforts to build an inclusive and supportive europe. i also hope very much that the slovenian presidency will inspire the next trio to include the issue of ageing in their priorities.

are working and that they are studying the cases, but we need more information. as far as the guidelines themselves are concerned, our report simply reiterates the regulation we negotiated. in fact, systemic or generalised violations must be considered. and we also recall that in article 3 of the regulation we have included a non-exhaustive list of indications of breach of the principles of the rule of law, and that of course the european commission can and should use any information available from a recognised institution. and we also believe that we should give civil society and ngos the law which must be understood in relation to other values and principles enshrined in article 2 of the treaty on european union. this was also in the rules. discrimination against minorities, attacks on freedom of the press, freedom of association or assembly, the independence of the judiciary, the proper functioning of the institutions to combat fraud, corruption, etc. - all of these can have a direct and sufficient impact on the union's budget. once we have clarified what we consider to be a breach of the rule of law and the impact it may have on the budget, we then talk about the measures, and here the regulation is very clear. articles 6 and 7: all stages and a precise timetable are laid down. it states that we must respect the principles of objectivity, non-discrimination and equal treatment, and that, in addition, the measures taken must be proportionate in nature, duration and gravity. it's all very clear. and finally, we end our contribution with the protection of the final recipients and beneficiaries. i would like to take this opportunity to congratulate not only my co-rapporteur but also the other groups in this house and to thank them for their work. the first idea we put on the table was the protection of the final beneficiaries. because the mechanism cannot penalise or prejudice these beneficiaries, and member states have an obligation, including the obligation to pay, to respect all agreements. in the agreement we reached with the council, and obviously with the commission, at the end of last year, the commission undertook to set up a system whereby beneficiaries could have access to all information and, above all, a system which would enable them, if necessary, to report irregularities. and in addition to this system, i hope that the commission is also working on how to use all the tools available to ensure that the funds are actually going to reach their intended recipients. so, commissioner, this debate is a good time to explain to us how they are working on this information and complaint portal, to explain to us also their view on the need for guidelines and their content, but i think this is the best opportunity for them to tell us exactly what they are doing and to answer the first question i asked in my speech: when are the first actions to be taken?

member of the commission. – mr president, i think it’s always good to continue our already traditional exchange on the rule of law conditionality mechanism today on the occasion of the own—initiative report on the guidelines today, so a first discussion in this format since we shared our draft for these guidelines with you and with member states, as it was done mid-june. this regulation is an historic achievement for the union and it applies since 1 january 2021 and has been followed up from that date, and may i recall that it was the commission’s proposal in 2018 to have such an instrument. again, i am grateful for all the support at least we received in this house before the european parliament elections, but also afterwards. having said this, again i can only recall that all relevant breaches that affect or risk affecting the sound financial management of the union budget and the financial interests of the union after that date will be covered. as said already in the past, no case will be lost. the commission has been actively working to assess information from all sources in view of building up a robust case, robust cases, and initiating the procedure under article 6 of the regulation. notification letters will be sent without any delay as soon as we have gathered concrete evidence that the conditions required by the regulation are fulfilled. the regulation requires the commission to provide guidance for the benefit of final recipients and beneficiaries whose rights have to be ensured, and on this we very much agree. as you know, our draft guidelines include such guidance. the guidelines also explain the procedure and the way the commission will assess cases under the regulation. i fully agree with your report that the guidelines cannot and will not change the law as set by the regulation, but only clarify how the commission will apply it. the regulation requires a sufficiently direct link between any rule of law breach and risks for the sound financial management of the union budget or the financial interests of the union. thus, a sober assessment of the following is therefore needed. the commission should assess whether a rule of law breach affects or seriously risks affecting the principles of sound financial management or the financial interests of the union in a sufficiently direct way. it may also need to assess whether the non-compliance with sound financial management principles arises from rule of law breaches in a sufficiently direct manner. if a sufficiently direct link with the budget cannot be established, the regulation will not apply. however, other tools of union law may apply instead, for example infringement procedures or the famous article 7 procedures. i would like to recall in particular that systematic or serious breaches are covered by the regulation but that a general indirect or merely theoretical effect on the budget is not enough to trigger the regulation. the commission must be able to demonstrate an identified or identifiable effect or risk for the budget. the regulation also requires the commission to apply the regulation in a complementary way. thus the procedure under the regulation will be opened when the substantive conditions described before are met, unless the commission finds that other procedures provided by the union’s financial sector regulation allow it to protect the budget more effectively than the general conditionality regulation. for instance, existing procedures to protect the union’s financial interests, including those involving investigations by olaf and eppo, as well as measures provided under the sector-specific financial rules, may be more effective and should be used instead. the regulation finally requires the commission to define the most appropriate and proportionate measures to be proposed to the council by evaluating the impact of the rule of law breach on the budget, taking into account all relevant factors. honourable members, the commission has received your letter calling for a full and immediate application of the regulation. you choose to pursue this path and of course the commission will react appropriately within the timeframe foreseen by the treaties. i will already state here that the commission has ensured proper application of the regulation since the day it entered into force. we have done so along two main strands. firstly, through the guidance on which you are consulted and that we are discussing today; secondly and most importantly, through the building up of the cases, which requires a well-formed, thorough, methodical and analytical assessment of the available information. for example, one of our sources in this context, the commission’s annual rule of law report, will be presented later this month. all this analytical work may soon materialise, demonstrating further the determination of the commission to apply the regulation in order to ensure an effective protection of the budget against breaches of the rule of law. in doing so, the commission will of course continue to take into account the views of parliament and this is also the reason why we are waiting for parliament’s comments on the guidelines under consultation, and be reassured once again, as mr sarvamaa said, i think we are strong allies and i think we are also allies in the way that we want this instrument to become a success story in a way that indeed it can help to address successfully and sustainably rule of law breaches and correct different and several developments in some of our member states in a way which we intend to see, at least here in the hemicycle, by a huge majority. so be reassured. we will act, but we will act in a way that finally we are successful. i think this is in all our interests.

madam president! the establishment in december 2020 of a global sanctions system by the european union for human rights violations, inspired by the so-called global magnitsky act in the us, should be seen positively. it significantly extends the union's sanctioning instruments and allows it to respond to cases of serious human rights violations. it is intended to improve the efficiency of their implementation. it is the fourth horizontal sanctions regime available to the union, following the regimes on terrorism, the use of chemical weapons and cyber-attacks. the system in question applies to acts such as genocide, crimes against humanity and other serious violations or abuses of human rights, including freedom of opinion and expression and freedom of religion or belief. we should consider extending the regime to corruption as well, as it is in the us. however, the call for the introduction of qualified majority voting for the adoption of sanctions under this system in place of the unanimity principle adopted by the council cannot be accepted. this would be another step towards limiting the rights of member states guaranteed by the treaties. smaller states have rights too, not just the big and powerful.
madam president, minister, i have to go. you will leave brussels for ljubljana today with a clear signal to the majority of this parliament that the principle of unanimity is ineffective. the principle that was supposed to give rights to the lesser, as it was said, makes it dangerous for us. it makes it unfortunate that one country is able to block decisions that serve the security of most countries in the european union. i stand before you as the representative of a nation that has already experienced such unanimity. the so-called liberum veto was in force in poland in the 17th century. we were a community with lithuania then, and also in security matters, you could block decisions then. it took unanimity. what did that lead to? chaos, anarchy, and finally, despite lasting only a year and a half, led to the dismemberment of our country, the domination of other powers and the complete collapse of our statehood. let this be a lesson and an example that you can use in the council in the future to abolish this principle of unanimity, which is completely unnecessary.
ladies and gentlemen! since the establishment of the global system of sanctions for human rights violations the european parliament and ngos call for the inclusion of abuses and corruption in the global sanctions system. corruption has a devastating impact on human rights, the proper functioning of states and societies, and on justice and the rule of law. i'm asking for the system to be expanded to include acts of corruption. i am in favour of the proposal for a qualified majority. we cannot allow a situation in which the imposition of sanctions is blocked by one country because of its political sympathies or economic interests. verification and control systems should not allow any breach to be missed and monitoring should be a permanent feature to ensure the best possible supervision of sanctioned entities. i believe that the european parliament does not play a proper role in this system, and that strengthening its role and providing oversight will increase the guarantee of the functioning of this system.
in writing. the adoption of an eu sanctions regime against human rights abusers worldwide is an important addition to the eu's human rights and foreign policy instruments and strengthens the union's role as a global human rights defender by enabling it to take restrictive measures against legal and natural persons involved in serious human rights violations worldwide. the list of specific serious human rights violations includes, inter alia, violations related to sexual and gender-based violence. it is important that member states interpret and apply sanctions in a uniform manner and that they comply with all relevant council decisions in this regard.
in writing. according to the eu treaties, the union's objective is to strengthen and support democracy, the rule of law, human rights and the principles of international law. however, this is a buzzword without the right tools to promote these goals. by imposing sanctions on members of administrations that violate human rights, the eu is able to promote its values and demonstrate that the eu does not tolerate the trampling of human rights, the rule of law and democracy. but the work is not yet done. the escape system is named after sergei magnitsky, who died in obscure circumstances in prison after investigating corruption in the russian government. however, at present, corruption is not a ground for sanctions. corruption is a major threat to the rule of law and it would be important that in the future, persons guilty of corruption could also be placed on a sanctions list. the role of the parliament in the preparation of sanctions should also be strengthened. furthermore, it should be important for the effectiveness of sanctions to ensure that the sanctions for infringements of sanctions are effective. the commission should therefore actively monitor that sanctions are not circumvented through various loopholes and that the sanctions achieve the objectives set for them. when sanctions are effective and proportionate, the mere fact of being deterred can prevent human rights violations.

president-in-office of the council. – mr president, for the past eight months, we have been following with concern the situation in ethiopia. the messages sent by the european union have been clear from the start. we have clearly condemned the situation and we have made additional efforts together with international partners, namely the united states, to put a halt to the violence in tigray. the recent offensive of the tigray defence forces and the fall of several towns, including mekelle, has changed the landscape in the tigray region with the ethiopian national defence forces moving out of the region. as far as we know, fighting still continues, albeit at a smaller level. in continuing their offensive, the tigray defence forces are meeting only low resistance. eritrean forces still seem to be present in the north and the amhara militia is controlling western tigray. we welcome the unilateral humanitarian ceasefire declared by the government as a step in the right direction, but it needs to be consolidated and accompanied by efforts from all parties to protect civilians and get humanitarian assistance in. the parties to the conflict have responsibilities also in these circumstances. we are assessing the situation on the ground. the four priorities that the eu has identified from the start of the crisis remain: first, to secure humanitarian access; second, to call all parties to protect civilians and to avoid further human rights violations; third, to ensure the withdrawal of eritrean troops from tigray; and, fourth, to establish a political dialogue for a sustainable solution. humanitarian access and the provision of humanitarian assistance remain the first priority: 91% of the population is in urgent need of assistance and 900 000 people face famine. there are worrying reports indicating a possible blockage of humanitarian deliveries. in order to protect civilians, we urgently need a full cessation of hostilities accepted by all parties. ethiopian troops have left most of tigray, but all parties must ensure the protection of civilians and assist the population. human rights abuses need to cease and also need to be investigated. we welcome the ongoing joint investigation by the office of the high commissioner on human rights and the ethiopian human rights commission. yesterday, the eu tabled a resolution in the human rights council to be sure that the high commissioner will be able to brief the human rights council accordingly. eritrean leaders and eritrean defence forces were asked to leave tigray. our leaders repeated that appeal in the european council on 25 june. asmara tells us that the eritrean defence forces are now at the eritrean—ethiopian border and do not engage in fighting unless provoked by the tigray people’s liberation front (tplf). what we see is that fighting has reduced in intensity, possibly an indication that the eritrean defence forces (edf) have indeed withdrawn from most of tigray. finally, we need a political solution through an inclusive dialogue organised by the ethiopian government in the whole of the country. the eu is ready to contribute to such a dialogue to preserve ethiopia’s integrity and unity. the country has just held federal and regional elections, which were overall peaceful and well organised. organising an inclusive national dialogue should be the next step. the foreign affairs council has discussed the situation regularly, notably in march, adopting conclusions, and in june. next week, on 12 july, we will come back to the matter. as i said, at its recent meetings the european council also addressed the issue. it condemned the ongoing atrocity, ethnic—based and sexual violence and other human rights violations in tigray, and welcomed the ongoing investigations to bring accountability and justice. it called for an immediate cessation of hostilities and impeded humanitarian access to all areas and, as i recalled before, the immediate withdrawal of eritrean forces. finally, it also reiterated the commitment of the eu and member states to support ethiopia in the implementation of democratic reform and reconciliation efforts.
member of the commission. – mr president, eight months into the conflict the european union remains extremely concerned at the situation in tigray. today, over five million children, women and men are through our humanitarian response efforts. together with our member states, we have mobilised almost eur 118 million in assistance to ethiopian refugees living in neighbouring sudan. my colleague, conditions that we have spelled out in a clear way need to be fulfilled before we can resume our financing and programming of our cooperation assistance. the european union has also called upon neighbouring leaders and like—minded partners to step up their efforts in support of the tigrayan people and to engage more actively to find a solution to the conflict. we support the joint investigation by the office of the un high commissioner for human rights and the ethiopian commission for human rights. we are ready to take concrete steps with international partners in order to situation in ethiopia. in conclusion, i wish to thank you for having facilitated this important debate, and i am looking forward to hearing your views and opinions.

the chairman of the council. ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, i thank you for your speeches, which have highlighted the importance of the geneva convention throughout the world, including, of course, the european union. i can assure you that the european union and its member states are aware of the importance of safeguarding the right to asylum and the principle of non-refoulement, as enshrined in this convention and also in the charter of fundamental rights of the european union. these fundamental principles must continue to be applied worldwide and to provide refuge and protection and to protect the physical integrity of persons in need of international protection or fleeing war, conflict or persecution. as you have seen, progress in this area is difficult to achieve in the european union. however, we must highlight important achievements such as the recent agreement to set up an asylum agency. the recent european council decisions have paid particular attention to the issue of migration. the conclusions call for enhanced cooperation with countries of origin and transit on the basis of mutually beneficial partnerships. member states invited the commission and the european external action service to prepare action plans for priority partner countries by autumn. i can assure you that the slovenian presidency will continue the work begun by its predecessors in the pact on migration and asylum, both in the legislative area and in the external dimension of migration.
this conversation is over. written declarations (article 171) the president of the court of justice shall be entitled to give a reasoned opinion.
in writing. the right to seek asylum is a fundamental human right guaranteed by the 1951 refugee convention. it is based on fundamental humanitarian values and is the cornerstone of eu asylum law. its principles, such as the principle of non-refoulement, have become part of customary international law, which means that countries that are not parties to the convention are obliged to comply with it. in the context of ongoing wars, conflicts and persecution, and record displacement, it has effectively protected the rights and lives of refugees for over seven decades. however, i do not agree that it is as relevant today as it was in 1951. one of the factors driving millions of people to migrate is the increasing climate change. but there is no category of climate refugees in international law. there is therefore a clear legal loophole that prevents the protection of this group of refugees. the definition of refugee in the 1951 convention does not apply to people displaced for environmental reasons. legally, we are not prepared for the coming waves of migrants. i therefore call for this anniversary to be an incentive to create and recognise an international definition of climate refugee, which will allow for the adoption of legislation to facilitate the procedure for granting refugee status to those who are fleeing, among other things, rising water levels.

member of the commission. – madam president, honourable members, let me start by warmly congratulating honourable member marques on this excellent report, which is a timely contribution to the review of the eu economic governance framework. as you know, we had originally launched a public consultation in february 2020, but had to put it on hold due to the onset of the pandemic. we have stated that we will relaunch the consultation when the economic recovery takes hold. we welcome the large support that this report has received in the committee on economic and monetary affairs (econ). this shows the cross-party support that exists on the importance of reviewing the economic governance framework, not least our common fiscal rules. it is also comforting that you succeeded to achieve broad convergence on this complex issue. the econ committee has produced a very rich report, and in the interest of time i will limit myself to a few key remarks. first, i am glad to note that the commission and the econ committee entirely agree on the near-term priorities for fiscal policy, namely to continue an expansionary fiscal stance for as long as is needed to support the recovery as well as the necessary transition of our economies, followed by a reorientation of fiscal policies aimed at fiscal sustainability in the medium term. this is entirely in line with the recent guidance that we provided to member states on 2 june. second, on the fiscal rules, the report correctly highlights the sharp increase in public debt in the eu since the start of the pandemic and the need to ensure country-specific pace of debt reduction that safeguards both fiscal sustainability and sustainable inclusive growth. we are not there yet, but once the health situation is fully under control and the economic recovery has taken hold, member states will indeed need to achieve a gradual and credible reduction of high public debt pressures, creating buffers for future needs and challenges. however, and turning to my third point, when the time comes for this gradual fiscal consolidation, we will need to avoid a mistake from the last crisis, which was to allow the burden of fiscal consolidation to fall on public investment. the recovery and resilience facility (rrf) will play a key role in this regard but member states must also seek to protect nationally financed public investment without jeopardising debt sustainability. the fiscal guidance that we recently provided to member states contains elements that go in this direction. the report rightly stresses that further efforts are needed to improve the quality of public finances so as to improve the country’s long-term debt sustainability and enhance the long-term growth potential. it is highly relevant to reflect how the eu’s economic governance framework could contribute to that. let me turn to the macroeconomic imbalance procedure (mip), which is another major element of our economic governance framework. the mip widened the scope of our surveillance beyond fiscal policies to cover other potential sources of macroeconomic imbalances such as large current account imbalances, deteriorating competitiveness, high private debt housing bubbles or fragile banking sectors. the covid-19 crisis has made some of those aspects even more relevant. there are indeed some challenges around mip implementation, on which we are collecting views. for instance, as highlighted also in our review, the policy traction of the mip has declined over time and some imbalances are only gradually being reduced. the report rightfully puts a specific emphasis on the euro area dimension. in recent years the commission already paid more attention to this such that all countries contribute to the rebalancing and their efforts are mutually reinforcing for the benefit of the area as a whole. in addition, the covid—19 crisis has called for a stronger forward-looking perspective in our mip surveillance, which we have pursued for this past year given the very unusual economic circumstances and exceptional uncertainty. to conclude, let me once again thank honourable member marques for this excellent and thought-provoking report. i look forward to hearing your views.

in writing. the political and humanitarian situation in lebanon has deteriorated further over the past year. the country is facing challenges from 1.5 million syrian refugees, food shortages, economic hardship and political instability. the circumstances of the explosion in beirut a year ago remain unclear, and those responsible have not been held accountable, causing significant social tensions. as maronite patriarch al-raï pointed out, corruption has plunged the country into its current crisis. we must support lebanon in overcoming this. after the civil war in lebanon, muslims and christians were able to resolve their conflicts with each other. today we are faced with a radically changed situation. we must take into account that lebanon is the center of the economic and banking sector in the middle east, so the current crisis could escalate into a regional crisis with unforeseen consequences. in the current uncertain political situation, there is a high risk that extremism will be encouraged. this must be prevented by any means necessary. the eu has a vital interest and historic responsibility in standing by lebanon. it is vital for the people of the country that eu support continues to reach communities in need efficiently and in a targeted manner after the madad fund is closed. this must be ensured when planning development aid.

member of the commission. – mr president, with today’s report, the european parliament shows once again its commitment towards the full inclusion of persons with disabilities. this is key to achieving a union of equality for all. i thank the rapporteur, mr alex agius saliba, the committee on petitions, the shadow rapporteurs and the other associated committees for their observations. the right to submit a petition to the european parliament is one of the fundamental rights recognised by the eu charter. petitions are also a precious source of information for the commission, for instance, in order to identify existing gaps. as your report points out, many barriers for persons with disabilities still remain, notably as regards accessibility, employment, education, the right to live independently in the community and mobility. i welcome your ideas and recommendations, and i look forward to our exchange today. we agree that adopting a human rights approach is essential to ensure that persons with disabilities can effectively participate in all fields of life on an equal basis with others. the new strategy for the rights of persons with disabilities that the commission adopted in march is our joint tool to improve the lives of people with disabilities in the eu and beyond in the next decade. embracing a human-rights approach, the strategy supports the eu in implementing the united nations convention on the rights of persons with disabilities and helps member states in their efforts. it takes into account the diversity of disability and promotes an intersectional perspective in its implementation, a point emphasised in your report. over the next years we will roll out a number of actions and flagship initiatives, notably to improve accessibility, independent living and access to services, free movement and labour market outcomes for persons with disabilities. these are among the key concerns raised in the petitions that the european parliament has examined and which your report highlights. eu funds, including under the cohesion policy and the recovery and resilience facility, will play a key role in achieving these objectives. as noted in your recommendations, the commission will continue to support member states in ensuring accessibility, which is a precondition for autonomy and equality. the european accessibility act has been a milestone. the commission will launch next year a european resource centre – accessible eu – to increase coherence and accessibility policies and facilitate access to relevant knowledge. fighting discrimination and barriers is our common goal. only half of all persons with disabilities are in employment, and this of course needs to change. we will step up our efforts in this area. next year, the commission will present a package to improve the labour market outcomes of persons with disabilities, seeking cooperation with the european network of public employment services, social partners and organisations of persons with disabilities. persons with disabilities have an equal right to live independently and be included in the community. by 2023, we will issue guidance recommending to member states improvements in this field. we agree that eu funds should support independent living, including the shift from institutions to services in the community. to improve service delivery for persons with disabilities and enhance the attractiveness of jobs in this area we will present by 2024 a framework for social services of excellence. persons with disabilities should enjoy all rights on an equal basis with others, including when moving to another member state. the commission will propose the creation, by 2023, of a european disability card. it will build upon the ongoing eu disability card pilot project, with a view to being recognised by all member states. i welcome your support for this initiative and stand ready to exchange further. to achieve these objectives and implement this strategy successfully, we need coordinated action at both national and eu level, with a strong commitment from member states and regional and local authorities. we will work closely with the member states, persons with disabilities and their representative organisations, the european parliament and stakeholders. we all have a responsibility to take the needs of persons with disabilities into consideration when designing, implementing and monitoring policies, legislation and funding programmes through targeted action and mainstreaming. as you reiterate in your report, we call on all eu institutions and bodies, agencies and delegations to designate disability coordinators for their institutions and for their disability strategies. i count on our continuous cooperation to make the union of equality a reality for the 87 million persons with disabilities in europe.

mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the covid-19 pandemic has not spared people with disabilities, whose situation has often worsened. i therefore welcome the opportunity to congratulate my colleague alex agius saliba and to discuss this own-initiative report, which has the merit of being based on multiple petitions on the issue of disability that have been addressed in recent years and which require a response, namely proposals for improving existing legislation and its better application. i would like to highlight a few of the valuable proposals which seem to be decisive for better protection of individuals at european level. firstly, the mutual recognition of the status of disabled person in the member states, which will finally remove a major obstacle to the right to free movement and to settle in another member state to work, study or for any other reason, with the prospect of developing a european card for disabled people by 2023. secondly, accessibility is a key issue. the 2019 directive has certainly been a step forward in harmonising accessibility requirements for certain products and services, but we need to go further and remove the persistent restrictions on its scope. finally, some advanced measures concern access to the labour market for disabled people. these are crucial ways of ensuring autonomy and dignity for all.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, as long as there is a debate or a provision on the rights of disabled people, it means that there is a problem and that there is still a lot to be done. this resolution highlights the responsibility of everyone to take action in defence of those who face obstacles and discrimination every day and are deprived of the freedoms and fundamental rights on which the european union is founded. today parliament is certainly taking a step forward to make the european union's action in defence of almost a quarter of its citizens who suffer from a form of disability even stronger and more credible. in this resolution, the european parliament does not limit itself to statements of principle, which are sometimes neglected or little considered, but commits the commission and the member states to take concrete action to improve the quality of life of many people with disabilities, but above all to remove the physical and cultural barriers that prevent social and economic inclusion and generate odious discrimination that undermines the fundamental right to equality. there are many points of agreement in this resolution, but i would like to stress the importance of the commitments made to prevent violence against women and the commitments made to overcome the employment and pay gap for women with disabilities, which adds to and amplifies the equally deplorable one affecting the entire female sex. finally, i would like to emphasize that this report is the result of numerous petitions submitted by many european citizens in the interests of millions of other citizens and confirms, in my view, the need for our parliament, as a directly elected body, to have the power of legislative initiative to express the interests of all the citizens who elected us.
mr president, the right to petition is one of the fundamental rights of every citizen and its functioning is important for participatory democracy itself. every year, many petitions concern the right of persons with disabilities in the european union. they point to the obstacles they face every day, to inaccessibility or discrimination. these petitions also help us to make our policies more responsive to their real needs. and although the right to petition is declared to be open to everyone, its exercise is tied to how accessible the petitioning processes themselves are. the information of citizens is also important in this respect, but also the question of how many people can actually exercise this right. that is why i would like to call again for us not to remain ambitious in ensuring accessibility not only to the right to petition but also to all other areas, but to take action. implement properly and timely legislation such as the web accessibility directive and the audiovisual directive. let's stop hiding behind a bunch of exceptions to the accepted rules of accessibility. and last but not least, we will use all the available finance, innovation, digitization and technological advances to make our society inclusive, barrier-free and to ensure full participation in it for everyone.

on behalf of the ecr group. - madam president! - i have to go. i'm not going to let you get away with this. the establishment of a new health security structure with specific responsibilities for critical medical precautions is to become one of the pillars of the security of the health union. the activities of the office are to be the main objective of strengthening the capacity of the european union and filling the gap in the eu system for response and preparedness to health emergencies. the principle of 'the best is the enemy of the good' is my guiding principle and as the rapporteur of the parliament responsible for extending the mandate of the ecdc, i am particularly interested in the synergies we can achieve with the participation and action of the existing agencies. it is necessary to provide for a precise distribution of the office's competences in order to avoid duplication and overlap of tasks carried out by other agencies and structures, so that so-called better solutions do not become competition with good actions taken so far. in addition, we need to have an explanation in the operational process of the office itself on how this synergy with the agencies will be further boosted by the crisis management mechanisms already in place. i believe that in order to achieve the objectives of the new office effectively, it is necessary to establish a close partnership and cooperation between all the european institutions and the member states by specifying the tasks of the hera management board, which will be composed of representatives of all the member states and of the institutions responsible for its functioning.
madam president, i believe my colleagues have already explained well why, as members of this parliament, we are so worried, but also angry, about the current proposal. we all want to strengthen the capacity of the eu to respond to health emergencies, but this process must be independent and driven only by public health interest. as foreseen now, the european health emergency preparedness and response authority (hera) will not be an independent agency. the commission will work directly with the industry on research, development and manufacturing of medicines. the only way to guarantee the independence of hera will be to include strict and binding policies on conflict of interest. we cannot afford, neither financially nor morally, that hera become an additional channel to give pharmaceutical companies a blank cheque. we have to draw the lessons from the so far poor experience of the eu public and private partnerships. we cannot afford to make the same mistakes for the credibility of the project, but also for the credibility of the european institutions.
madam president, madam commissioner, we cannot simply discuss in this house today the role of the european parliament in the hera. there are many other issues which are objectively more relevant if we are to have this new authority effective, operational and useful in managing some 50 billion euros by 2027 in four months. health is a matter for the member states. we therefore need to know the structure and functioning of this authority, the mechanisms for coordination with the states, the instruments that are to be put at the service of hera to ensure the availability, access and distribution of medicines. what are the commission's plans to ensure that there is no overlap of powers with agencies whose mandates have just been extended, such as the ema or the ecdc? in short, commissioner, we will support efforts to develop a european pharmaceutical industry and improve our capacity for research and for responding to health emergencies. but we need guarantees to prevent good ideas from turning into giant structures which add no value to the european citizen and which blur the sovereignty of nations.
madam president, commissioner, do we need a european emergency health authority? most likely, yes. but do we need it to be a private office of the european commission that can negotiate directly with pharmaceutical companies and the private sector, without transparency, without democracy, without parliament? no, i'm not going. were there gaps in the management of the pandemic? there have been, and several. and they also have to do with the fact that we have divested from national health services, because there have been cuts often imposed by european policies. they also fail to give due weight to the agencies we already have, namely the european medicines agency and the ecdc. so we need an articulated response, certainly, but responding to health crises and health emergencies is also about strengthening national health services, the response of professionals, and investing in scientific research and science. we cannot accept in any way a european agency, a european authority, which answers these questions without us knowing how or why, without us knowing what its role is, without us knowing what its mandate is, and without the citizens being able to be heard.

madam president! ladies and gentlemen! i agree with the common strategic vision of achieving cyber resilience in the union. today, these capacities are fragmented and their consolidation and coordination is a task for the near future. experts confirm that the european union has a significant, fully operational capability to ensure cyber resilience and collective rapid response to cyber incidents. therefore, it is necessary to exchange information between cybersecurity crisis response teams, to exchange best practices, and to intensify training, research and exercises. a european fast and secure network for detecting, assessing and countering cyber-attacks is needed. and that is why i agree with the recommendations that have been made, which are very important and need to be emphasised, including, among other things, raising public awareness and improving citizens' skills in defending against cyberattacks and closer cooperation between the european union and nato, especially in the field of interoperability of cyber defence.

in writing. – over the past years, cyber risks and vulnerabilities have increased. cyberspace has become the fifth domain of warfare alongside the traditional military spaces. in this area, the eu is still subject to many cyberattacks, deeply harming its citizens. the world economic forum stresses that the number of countries experiencing cyberattacks has increased by 150% between 2017 and 2019. i support the commission president proposal in her latest state of the union address, to develop a european cyber-defence policy and a cyber-resilience act. these capacities are now fragmented and their consolidation and coordination must be a strategic objective of our mandate. i call for the members states to strengthen their responses against cyber threats through an efficient, collective and rapid response mechanism, within the eu framework but also through nato, thus gathering all necessary actors to efficiently fight against cyber vulnerabilities.

member of the commission. madam president, madam chairman of the committee on transport and tourism, if i may, dear karima, ladies and gentlemen, first of all, thank you for giving me the opportunity i told you. it is also no coincidence that three of the four member states with the best tourist performance this summer are among the countries which started using the digital certificate as soon as july and august 2021. thanks to this, many coastal destinations, especially rural ones, have welcomed more residents from neighbouring countries, thus compensating for the loss of travellers from north america or the asia-pacific regions. the european digital certificate has also encouraged airlines to finally reopen their routes and increase their offerings, thus improving our intra-european air connectivity. compared to 2019, the number of air routes served by our european airports increased from -57% in april to -16% in august. this is confirmed by a eurobarometer survey published in september 2021. for 65% of those surveyed, or almost two thirds, the european certificate is currently the most effective tool to facilitate travel within europe. that's how they see it. as for on behalf of the ecr group. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. ladies and gentlemen! in the cohesion policy package, the european commission proposed a new mechanism to remove legal and administrative barriers in a cross-border context. this tool, as established at union level, would allow the application of the legislation of one member state in a neighbouring country with the agreement of the competent authorities. studies of border areas show that they are economically worse off than other regions. access to various public services is more difficult. different legal and administrative systems generate additional costs for cooperation. the proposed legal solution to its mission is therefore worthy of support, especially since interreg crossborder cooperation programmes are not a sufficient tool to reduce existing barriers. however, the detailed arrangements contained in the draft regulation require further analysis. many of the rules require explanation because they are vague. if a member state chooses to apply the mechanism of the proposed regulation, one of two solutions is possible. the first is the conclusion of a european crossborder commitment, whereby certain provisions of a member state are applied in the territory of a neighbouring country. the second solution is to sign a european cross-border declaration. the authority signing the declaration undertakes to initiate legislative work within a specified timeframe to make the necessary changes to the legislation in force. there are many doubts about the first solution. the effect of the undertaking is to maintain the existing national rules. however, in the context of the implementation of a specific cross-border project, the undertaking allows for a derogation from these provisions. instead, the law of the neighbouring country will apply. hence the doubt as to whether this pathway could be applied to projects involving entities from the undertaking country. the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed solution is also questionable. a lengthy and multi-stage procedure for triggering the mechanism may prove to be of little help to the initiator of a cross-border project.

mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, today's debate confirms that asbestos, despite its prohibition, is still a serious problem. unfortunately, it was said, many citizens still die and many more are affected by diseases resulting from exposure to asbestos, many of which are not even recognized as occupational diseases and therefore do not entitle the victims and their families to any compensation. i thank rapporteur villumsen and all the colleagues who have worked on this report, which makes it possible to update european legislation, especially, as has been said, in the light of the measures with which europe is promoting the renovation and regeneration of the building stock, which is why it is necessary to introduce the obligation to check for the presence of asbestos and subsequently remove it before any work is started, as well as a mandatory certification attesting to the absence or regularity of asbestos before a sale or a lease for buildings built before 2005. in the light of the new measures which the commission will be presenting, i should like to draw attention to a few points. first of all, it is necessary to identify among the occupational diseases all those which are objectively and scientifically linked to exposure to asbestos. if we really want to remove asbestos, we must reduce bureaucracy and provide financial support for property owners, and adequate training for technicians and workers. finally, non-invasive techniques should be encouraged so that the risk factor is reduced completely even at the screening stage. let us remember that investing in screening, but above all in the removal and purification of asbestos, means investing in the health of our citizens.
mr president, i would like to thank you. up to 35 million buildings in the eu will need to be renovated by 2035. there's going to be a wave of green renovations that will lead to huge energy savings. but if we're not careful, the renovations will also bring a wave of cancer. a wave that will cost thousands of europeans their lives because the buildings contain asbestos, which is a deadly substance. we have a limit today, yes, but it is not high enough. we have a screening effort, it's just too bad. we have legislation, yes, but we lack enforcement. that means there's still some life-threatening asbestos dust. it gives workers cancer that takes their lives. this is unacceptable. we need to lower the threshold. we need to improve the screening of buildings before renovations begin and we need to ensure that there is more control. it's not right for people to put their lives on the line to take care of their jobs. asbestos has already cost many lives. let's make sure this ends now, before the next generation loses their lives.
mr. chairman, please! although the production and placing on the market of asbestos has been banned in the union since 2005, the existing surveillance tools do not guarantee that products containing asbestos do not enter the european market. it is also still present in many of the buildings around us, posing a serious health threat to millions of european citizens. nearly 50 000 people die every year in the union from this disease. in the interests of the safety and lives of citizens, we call on the commission to take decisive legislative action, as at present only some member states have adequate plans to remove existing asbestos stocks. the european union should be more active in encouraging member states to take action by offering them real support and assistance in detecting and removing asbestos. it should also lay down measures to protect workers and consumers from the harmful effects of that substance. the commission's initiative is both possible and desirable, especially since the issue of safe asbestos removal can now be co-financed by european funds under the green deal and the reconstruction fund.
mr. chairman, please! in the wake of covid-19, the governments of the union's member states have taken a number of decisions that have triggered a crisis in many areas of social and economic life. they have also had a major impact on cultural activities in a broad sense and on the situation of artists and cultural workers. the closure of cultural institutions, the cancellation of cultural events and artistic routes, the closure of educational institutions, the suspension of many artistic cooperation projects and, finally, the closure of national borders have had the greatest impact on the situation of artists. and yet, the lives of those who practice the arts are characterized by a lack of stability and a permanent basis for existence. the covid crisis has changed the professional activity of artists. many of them remained or are still without adequate remuneration or without remuneration at all. we should therefore ensure that the budget for culture is increased, that access to funding for cultural projects is increased and that administrative burdens are reduced. the union's competence in this area is limited, but as far as possible within the legal framework, let us promote culture. the artistic profession deserves special treatment and protection.
in writing. – the covid-19 crisis heavily disrupted the cultural and creative sectors and brought some of them to a complete halt for an extended period of time. this situation exacerbated the atypical and all too often precarious working conditions of artists and cultural workers. creative industry associations have called, since the beginning of this crisis in the eu and its member states, for urgent financial support in order to withstand the crisis and, most importantly, so they can recover in the post-crisis period. further steps need to be taken to protect the european film and audiovisual sector, media, publishers, the music industry or content creators in different areas. we call on the member states to ensure full access to social protection for artists and cultural workers, regardless of their employment status, and ask the commission to propose a european status of the artist setting out a common framework for working conditions and minimum standards common to all eu. creative and cultural industries account for almost 10% of romania’s gdp with over 400 thousand employees. it is of the upmost importance to protect the most vulnerable sectors of our society and economy so that we can recover from this time of crisis.

member of the commission. mr president, first of all, dear mrs melbārde, i warmly welcome your report. i am pleased that parliament and the commission are working together to support the media and audiovisual sector, which are fundamental to our democracies and our cultural diversity, and which we talked a lot about in the previous debate. there are many points of convergence between this report and the commission's approach, as detailed in our action plans for european democracy, as well as for the media and audiovisual. the scale of your report shows how many and complex the challenges in the audiovisual and media field are today. in the face of these challenges, our strategy is based on three pillars: regulation to protect and guide, funding to strengthen and develop, and transformation and innovation to conquer and shine. regarding regulation, our strategy is to establish rules of the game adapted to the digital age. i would like to highlight three initiatives aimed at ensuring fair competition. the audiovisual media services directive places obligations on platforms to set quotas for the exhibition of works and also allows for financial obligations to be imposed on them. the new copyright rules encourage creativity and transparency in the digital space, while protecting freedom of expression. it is particularly important that member states transpose and apply this new regulatory framework. similarly, with our proposals on digital services and the digital markets regulation (the dsa and dma), europe has taken the initiative to clarify the responsibilities of platforms. i should also mention a new regulatory project aimed at protecting media pluralism and freedom: as announced here by the president of the commission, we are preparing a draft media freedom law, the media freedom act, which will be proposed next year. on the financial side of our strategy, the commission has set out its vision in a plan for the recovery and transformation of the media and audiovisual sectors. in the context of the covid-19 crisis, which has hit some media so hard, this plan brings together the various tools at our disposal. an unprecedented effort has been provided with the next generation eu recovery plan, whether through national recovery plans or through framework programmes from the european budget. several member states have included the audiovisual sector as a priority in their recovery plan. on the other hand, the commission has made significant progress in preparing and implementing the concrete actions provided for in the action plan. first, we have published an interactive tool online to help businesses participate in the various european programmes to support the audiovisual and media sectors under the new budgetary framework. as for the audiovisual sector, we are launching media invest, an equity investment platform. the objective is to mobilise investments of eur 400 million over a seven-year period, thus making a significant contribution to filling the equity financing gap of independent producers and distributors. for the first time, thanks to the strong support of the parliament, our creative europe programme is funding projects related to media pluralism. this is important, but as the report underlines, more effort is needed. this is why we are also developing alternative and sustainable sources of funding for the news media, including through a pilot project, under the investeu programme, to co-invest with foundations and other private partners. we pay special attention to local media. we strongly agree on the need to strengthen support for media education. the commission will step up its efforts, for example by supporting national media education campaigns, in cooperation with the european observatory on digital media. finally, innovation in the media is essential. this is why we are mobilising the horizon europe and digital europe programmes. we're going to launch a data space that allows collaboration and sharing of audience or content data and metadata. ownership, control and exploitation of data are key for media creators and companies. the commission will therefore launch a dialogue with the audiovisual industry in the coming weeks to explore possible actions to improve access to and availability of audiovisual content in the european union. if we want to be stronger, we must think europe, think at the level of the continent and of a single market for creativity, but also for the protection of the media, because without a free media, democracy is in danger.

the agenda includes the brief presentation of the report by corina crețu, on behalf of the committee on budgetary control, on the effectiveness with which member states have used eu funds through the solidarity fund in the event of natural disasters (2020/2127 ((ini)) (a9-0273/2021).
the reporter. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the european union solidarity fund is, in fact, living proof that the european union is already a very real presence in the lives of all its citizens. whether it is the earthquakes in italy, the fires in greece and portugal or the floods in romania, this fund has shown that solidarity between european countries is essential, especially in times of crisis. to get the big picture, a few concrete figures would be helpful: the european solidarity fund has mobilised over eur 6,5 billion for 96 natural disaster situations in 23 member states and one acceding country between 2002 and 2020. the largest number of claims was for flood damage, at around 60%, followed by earthquakes, but unfortunately the solidarity fund was not conceived at the time of its launch as an emergency instrument and therefore over time more and more member states have asked for the procedures to be carried out much faster. that is why in this report, i called for the fund to become more flexible and more effective in delivering financial assistance to states affected by natural disasters in a timely manner. the procedures for obtaining financial support need to be simplified, the time taken to allocate funds reduced, and the use of funds more rigorously controlled. at this hour, the time elapsed from a disaster to the payment of the respective sums is about one year. that is why i think, ladies and gentlemen, that in view of the crisis we are going through, it is welcome that this fund has been extended to emergency situations in countries facing health crises. the introduction of covid-related expenditure has led to a doubling of solidarity fund expenditure, which in july this year alone was estimated at over eur 3 billion. so we always have to think about simplification, but also about control. let us not forget, for example, that in emergency situations such as these, public procurement is a vulnerable area to fraud, corruption and irregularities, which is why the report also stresses the need to make control systems more efficient. in view of all the above, we believe that the european commission should propose more effective proactive solutions, in particular by continuing its work towards simplified use of the solidarity fund. in order to ensure that the solidarity fund achieves the purpose for which it was designed from the outset, it is necessary, in our opinion, to revise it. i would like to take this opportunity to express my deepest sympathy to all european citizens and their families who have been affected by natural disasters or the health crisis we are currently experiencing.
member of the commission. – mr president, i would like to thank parliament and the rapporteur, ms crețu, for the report and for the appreciation of the eu solidarity fund as an important instrument of the eu. solidarity is a core value upon which the union is built. the eu solidarity fund was created to provide eu solidarity by contributing to post-disaster relief in member states and accession countries confronted with devastating natural disasters and major public health emergencies. since its creation, the fund has mobilised close to eur 7 billion for interventions in a hundred disaster events in 24 countries. a recent evaluation of the eu solidarity fund confirmed the effectiveness of the fund and the synergies between the eu solidarity fund and other eu policy instruments for disaster risk management. it also concluded that the fund brings clear eu added value and demonstrates eu solidarity in action. however, we cannot ignore that climate change is causing more frequent and intense weather and climate-extreme disasters in europe and around the world. the past two years have provided a sad truth. heatwaves, drought, forest fires, floods, earthquakes, are breaking records every year in both rate and intensity, with a disastrous impact on human lives, the economy and on ecosystems. between 2002 and 2019, the fund was mobilised for 91 interventions. in comparison, in 2020 alone the commission received 31 new fund applications. for the first time ever, the fund was mobilised not only following natural disasters, but also in response to the covid-19 public health emergency. of these, 19 members states and three enlargement candidates will receive fund assistance by the end of 2021 to respond to the covid-19 public health emergency. and this year, the commission has so far received eight eu solidarity fund (eusf) applications for support to recover from natural disasters. we should also be concerned about the increasing intensity and impact of the disasters. last year, croatia received eusf assistance of over 680 million, the second highest amount ever paid by the fund for emergency and recovery operations after a natural disaster. this year the application from germany for the devastating floods in july reported the biggest total direct damage ever presented in the history of the fund – eur 29.2 billion. this is the damage suffered by germany alone. belgium, the netherlands, austria and luxembourg also submitted applications following this summer’s natural disasters. the commission has started the assessment of these applications in order to have a comprehensive overview of the needs. based on this assessment, the commission will consider all possible options within our instruments to allow the eusf to continue to deliver on eu solidarity to member states. the increasing number and scale of natural disasters in the last two years, as well as the need to provide assistance in relation to the covid-19 public health emergency, has put a severe strain on the resources set aside for the fund, as agreed by the legislators in the 2021-2027 multiannual financial framework (mff). moreover, contrary to the commission’s mmf proposal to restore the eusf envelope of eur 1 billion, the instrument was integrated into the new solidarity and emergency aid reserve, with the total amount of eur 1.2 billion shared with the emergency aid reserve. mobilisation of the resources is today more challenging as it also covers other eu internal and external emergencies, while calls are likely to grow, as has been painfully illustrated this summer. the eu cannot be asked to choose between competing needs for relief and recovery at home or abroad. we must be in a position to provide support to both member states and those in need elsewhere. in any case, the commission remains determined to support member states to speed up assessment and application procedures and deliver on eu solidarity with the eusf.
the debate is closed. the vote will take place on tuesday 19 october 2021. the commission shall be assisted by the committee of the regions.
in writing. analysis of the data provided by the commission on disbursements from the fund shows that the fund pays out in a geographical key. romania, which is particularly vulnerable to seasonal flooding, has submitted 8 aid applications since 2005. the cumulative value of its losses to date was estimated at eur 4 billion, and the fund paid it approximately eur 130 million in compensation. france has benefited from the fund seven times since 2002. its losses were estimated at around eur 9 billion, despite only one natural disaster being of national scope, i.e. affecting more than one region. in romania, 4 disasters were classified as nationwide, france received about 120 million more than romania. austria applied for aid in 2002 following the floods, the losses were estimated at around eur 3 billion, and the commission paid it eur 134 million in compensation. eight years later, poland, with similar flooding and damage, as the damage was also estimated at 3 billion euros, received 29 million less than austria. the data above show that the commission favours the countries of the old union, inter alia by overstating the amount of the losses, which consequently leads to higher compensation payments. this practice needs to change if the fund is to be truly solidarity-based.
