good day to you all. i call the court to order. we shall now move on to the first item on the agenda: council and commission statements on the crisis of the rule of law in poland and the primacy of european union law (2021/2935 (rsp)).
president-in-office of the council. – mr president, thank you for organising this debate. respect for the rule of law is critical to guarantee the proper functioning of the union. the european union is a union of law, and the primacy of eu law is the foundation of it. in eu architecture, primacy of eu law is the way to guarantee the equality of member states before the treaties and to ensure that all union citizens enjoy the same rights. without primacy, the application of eu law would vary from one member state to another. this would destroy the level playing field in the single market. it is also a precondition for daily interaction and for smoothly resolving disputes. it is, ultimately, the basis for our living together in a common european home. the presidency is committed to bringing forward exchanges in a positive and constructive atmosphere on rule of law and related issues. today, at the general affairs council, in the framework of the annual rule of law dialogue, ministers will be discussing developments in the area of rule of law in a general horizontal debate. the commission’s 2021 rule of law report fits into this exercise, and the primacy of eu law is among the topics covered in the report. the general affairs council will discuss again rule of law issues at its session on 23 november. a country–specific discussion will cover developments in five main member states, namely: croatia, cyprus, italy, latvia and lithuania. the council also remains seized of the article 7 teu procedure. the presidency is committed to advancing these proceedings in a council in december. in addition, the council continues to closely monitor the recent rule of law developments in poland. we aspire for a constructive dialogue between the commission and poland, which would lead towards converging positions. we will also continue this discussion within the council. i look forward to your intervention today, and to hearing prime minister morawiecki on how poland sees the way forward.
president of the commission. – mr president, almost 40 years ago, in december 1981, the communist regime in poland imposed martial law. many members of solidarność, the independent trade union, and of other groups were put in jail, simply because they stood up for their rights. the people of poland wanted democracy, like millions of other europeans from budapest to tallinn to east berlin. they wanted the freedom to choose their government, they wanted free speech and free media, they wanted an end to corruption, and they wanted independent courts to protect their rights. the people of central and eastern europe wanted to join the european family of free people, a strong community of values and democracy. because that is what europe is about and that is what europe stands for. the recent ruling of the polish constitutional court puts much of this into question. we have been concerned about the independence of the judiciary for some time. judges have seen their immunity being lifted and have been driven out of office without justification, and this threatens judicial independence, which is a basic pillar of the rule of law. we have taken a number of measures. we continue to have a regular dialogue. but unfortunately the situation has worsened. and this is not only the commission’s opinion, this is what has been confirmed by the european court of justice and the european court of human rights. and now this has culminated in the most recent ruling of the polish constitutional court. the european commission is, at the moment, carefully assessing this judgment, but i can already tell you today that i am deeply concerned. this ruling calls into question the foundations of the european union. it is a direct challenge to the unity of the european legal order. only a common legal order provides equal rights, legal certainty, mutual trust between member states and, therefore, common policies. this is the first time ever that the court of a member state finds that the eu treaties are incompatible with the national constitution. this has serious consequences for the polish people because the ruling has a direct impact on the protection of the judiciary. the ruling undermines the protection of the judicial independence, as guaranteed by article 19 of the treaty and as interpreted by the european court of justice. without independent courts, people have less protection and consequently their rights are at stake. polish people must be able to rely on fair and equal treatment in the judicial system, just like any other european citizen. in our union, we all enjoy the same rights and this basic principle fundamentally impacts people’s lives because, if european law is applied differently in grenoble or göttingen or gdańsk, eu citizens would not be able to rely on the same rights everywhere. when joining the european union, the polish people put their trust in the european union. they expected the european union to defend their rights, and rightly so. the commission is the guardian of the treaty. it is my commission’s duty to protect the rights of eu citizens wherever they live in our union. the rule of law is the glue that binds our union together. it is the foundation of our unity. it is essential for the protection of the values on which our union is founded: democracy, freedom, equality and respect for human rights. this is what all 27 member states have signed up to as part of this union, as sovereign countries and free people. we cannot – and will not – allow our common values to be put at risk. the commission will act, and the options are all known. the first option are infringements, where we legally challenge the judgment of the polish constitutional court. another option is the conditionality mechanism and other financial tools. the polish government has to explain to us how it intends to protect european money, given this ruling of their constitutional court because, in the coming years, we will be investing eur 2 100 billion with the multiannual budget and the nextgenerationeu recovery programme. this is european taxpayers’ money and, if our union is investing more than ever to advance our collective recovery, we must protect the union’s budget against breaches of the rule of law. the third option is the article 7 procedure. this is the powerful tool in the treaty, and we must come back to it because, let me remind you, the polish constitutional court that today has cast doubts on the validity of our treaty is the same court that, under article 7, we consider not to be independent and legitimate. this, in many ways, comes full circle. i deeply regret that we find ourselves in this situation. i have always been a proponent of dialogue and i will always be. this is a situation that can and must be resolved. we want a strong poland in a united europe. we want poland to be at the heart of our debates in building a common future. poland has a stake in europe. together, we can build a europe that is strong and confident in a world where other big powers become more and more assertive. europe has benefited from poland’s unique experience so much. without the people of poland, our european journey would have been very different. when karol wojtyła, as pope john paul ii, went to his homeland, he changed european history forever. when lech wałęsa, with a scattered group of trade unionists, overcame a mighty army, we saw the beginning of the fall of the iron curtain. and when president lech kaczyński ratified the lisbon treaty, together with the charter of fundamental rights, he reaffirmed poland’s commitment to our values. polish people have played a fundamental role in making our union whole, in enabling their homeland to thrive as a vital part of our union, and they will always be. polsko, jesteś i zawsze będziesz w sercu europy! niech żyje polska, niech żyje europa! poland, you are, and you will always be, at the heart of europe. long live poland and long live europe!
prime minister of poland. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. madam president! ladies and gentlemen of the house! i stand before you today in parliament to develop our position on a number of fundamental issues which i consider to be fundamental to the future of the european union. and not just for the future of poland, but for the future of our union as a whole. first, i'll talk about the crises that europe faces today and that we need to address. second, i'm going to talk about standards and rules that should be the same for everyone, and all too often are not. thirdly, i will give my view on the principle that no public authority should take action for which there is no legal basis. the fourth point of my speech will be about the polish constitutional tribunal judgment and what this judgment and other similar judgments mean for the union, as well as the importance of diversity and mutual respect. and then, in the fifth, i'm going to present our view of constitutional pluralism. i will then point out the huge risks to society as a whole that arise from the application of the judgment of the court of justice of the european union, which are already materializing in poland. and finally, in the end, i'm going to summarize all of the conclusions and look, i think, with hope into the future. i'm going to start with the fundamental issues, the challenges that are crucial to our common future. the high chamber, social inequalities, inflation, rising living costs that affect all europeans, external threats, rising public debt, illegal immigration and the energy crisis, all add to the climate challenge, and all translate into social unrest and a long list of powerful problems. the debt crisis has raised the question for the first time since the war whether we can provide a better life for future generations. the situation around our borders is becoming more and more unstable: in the south, the rebellion of millions of people has turned the mediterranean basin into a tragic place. in the east we are faced with the aggressive policy of russia, which is even going to war to block the choice of the european path among the countries of our neighbourhood. today, we are on the verge of a major gas and energy crisis. the rapidly rising prices, caused by deliberate actions by russian companies among others, are already forcing many european companies to choose between reducing production or passing costs on to consumers. the scale of this crisis could shake europe in the coming weeks. many businesses could go bankrupt, and millions of households, tens of millions of people could be pushed into poverty and scarcity by the gas crisis through uncontrolled cost increases across europe. there's also the risk of dominoes. one crisis can cascade into another. i say "we" every time, because none of these things are solvable by ourselves. not all of these problems have affected my country as dramatically as they have in other countries of the union. but that doesn't change the fact that i consider all of these problems to be our problems. i'd like to say a few words about poland's contribution to our joint project. european integration is a civilization and a strategic choice for us. we want to make europe strong again, ambitious and courageous. so we're not just looking at the short-term benefits, but also what we can give europe. poland benefits from integration primarily through trade in the common market. technology transfers and direct transfers are also very important, but poland did not enter the union empty-handed. the process of economic integration has expanded the possibilities for companies in my country, but it has also opened up huge opportunities for german, french and dutch companies. businesses in these countries have benefited enormously from the enlargement of the union. just count the outflow, the huge outflow of dividends, interest earnings and other financial instruments. from the countries of central europe, the less wealthy ones to the countries of western europe, the more wealthy ones. but we want to make sure that there are no losers in this partnership, only winners. poland was the promoter of an ambitious reconstruction fund, so that today's response to the challenges of climate, energy, post-pandemic transformation is adequate to the needs, so that economic growth is strong, that it gives hope and does not leave millions of children, women and men defenseless against globalization. we have spoken with one voice with the european parliament on these matters. poland strongly supports the single european market, we want strategic autonomy strengthening the 27 countries. poland or germany, the czech republic and other central european countries are therefore promoting solutions that increase the competitiveness of the european economy in the spirit of enforcing the four fundamental freedoms. free movement of goods, services, capital and people, without encouraging the kind of tax haven activities that some western european countries unfortunately still do, and in this way they are disgracing their neighbours. yes, your honor, the tax havens we tolerate in the union are the taking of money by the richest. is that fair? does it help improve the lot of the middle class or the less fortunate? is this in the catalogue of european values? i doubt that very much. poland and central europe also support an ambitious enlargement policy that will strengthen europe in the western balkans and complete european integration geographically, historically and strategically. we want the union's global aspirations and we are in favour of a strong european defence policy in a structure fully consistent with nato. today, when the eastern border of the union is the target of an organised attack cynically using migration from the middle east to destabilise, poland is the security of europe, providing, together with lithuania and latvia, the bulwark that protects that border, and by strengthening our defence capability we are strengthening the security of the union in the most traditional sense. standing before you today, i would like to thank the polish, lithuanian and latvian services, as well as all the southern european countries, our border guard and uniformed services for their hard work and professionalism in protecting the union's borders. security has many dimensions. today, with all of us feeling the effects of rising gas prices, we can see clearly the results of shortsightedness in energy security. gazprom's policy and the approval of nord stream 2 are already translating into record gas prices. while today in the countries that founded the communities, the level of trust in the union has fallen to historically low levels, such as 36% in france, in poland trust in europe remains at the highest level: more than 85% of polish citizens clearly say that poland is and will remain a member of the union. my government and the parliamentary majority which supports it are part of that pro-european majority in poland. this does not mean that poles today do not have doubts and worries about the direction of change in europe. this concern is obvious and unfortunately justified. i've talked about how much poland has brought to the union, but unfortunately we still hear about the division into the better and the worse. we have too often had to deal with a europe of double standards. and now i'm going to tell you why we need to end this model. today, all europeans expect one thing from us: they want us to face the challenges posed by several crises at once, not against each other, not by forcibly seeking out those who are not guilty, or rather those who are not guilty but who are conveniently blamed. unfortunately, in view of certain practices in the union's institutions, many citizens of our continent are now asking themselves: what do the extremely different decisions and judgments of brussels and luxembourg mean for different member states, which are made in similar circumstances and which in fact perpetuate the division between the countries of the strong, the old and the new union, between the strong and the weak? is that really equality? pretending that problems don't exist has very bad consequences. the citizens are not blind, they are not deaf. if complacent politicians and officials fail to see this, they will gradually lose confidence, and with them, the institutions. and it is already happening, your highness. politics must be based on principles. the principle which we in poland recognize as the foundation of the european union is the principle of democracy. that is why we cannot remain silent when our country, also in this room, is being attacked in an unjust and biased way. the rules of the game must be the same for all, and they are the responsibility of all, including the institutions that have been established by these treaties. that's what the rule of law is all about. it is unacceptable to extend the powers of the court, to act on the basis of established facts. it is unacceptable to impose one's decision on others without a legal basis. the use of the language of financial blackmail, the use of words like penalties or even more extreme language against certain member states is all the more unacceptable. the member states. that's not how democracies work. we are a proud country. poland is one of the countries with the longest history of statehood and democratic development. three times in the 20th century, at great cost, we fought for the freedom of europe and the world. in 1920, saving berlin and paris from the bolshevik onslaught. then in 1939, going first to the murderous battle with germany, with the third reich, which affected the fate of this war. finally, in 1980, when solidarity gave hope to overthrow another totalitarianism, the cruel communist system. the post-war reconstruction of europe was made possible by the sacrifices of many nations, but not all of them could benefit from it. high lsbo, now a word about the rule of law. but there are many ways to talk about the rule of law, and each one will have a different understanding of the concept to some degree. but i think most of us would agree that there can be no rule of law without a few conditions, without the principle of separation of powers, without the independence of the courts, without respecting the principle that every power has limits, limited competence, and also without respecting the hierarchy of sources of law. union law takes precedence over national law up to the level of statute and in areas of competence conferred on the union. this is the case in all eu countries, but the constitution remains the supreme law. if the institutions set up by the treaties exceed their powers, member states must have the tools to respond. the union is a great achievement of the countries of europe and a strong economic, political and social alliance. it is the strongest, most developed international organization in history. but the european union is not a state. the country is the 20 member states of the union. it is the states that remain european sovereigns, that are the masters of the treaties, and that determine the extent of the competences conferred on the european union. we have given the union a very large range of powers in the treaties, but we have not told it everything. many areas of law remain the competence of national states. we have no doubt that european law takes precedence over national law in all areas where the member states have conferred competences on the union. however, like the courts of many other countries, the polish court questions whether the court of justice's monopoly on the actual boundaries of the conferral of these powers is a correct solution. since the determination of this scope is a constitutional matter, someone must also comment on the constitutionality of such possible new competences. especially when the court of justice is drawing from the treaties ever new competences for the eu institutions. otherwise, it would be pointless to insert article 4 of the treaty of union, which says that the union shall respect the political and constitutional structures of the member states. it would be pointless to insert in the treaty article 5, which says that the union can only act within the limits of the powers conferred, granted. both articles would be empty yes, empty if no one but the court of justice could comment on the constitutional conditions of the domestic order. your honour, i am aware that the recent ruling of the polish constitutional court has been the subject of a fundamental misunderstanding. if i had heard that the constitutional court of another country had annulled the eu treaties, i would have been surprised too, but above all i would have tried to find out what the court actually decided. and it is also for this reason that i have asked to be heard in this debate today, to present to you what is really at issue, and that is not to make up stories of polemics or lies for political reasons about alleged violations of the rule of law. so in the next section of my talk, i want to present the facts to you, and to do that, i'd best go straight to a few quotes. first, in the national legal order, the primacy of eu law does not apply to the provisions of the constitution. this constitution is at the top of the domestic legal system. secondly, the principle of the primacy of community law must not undermine the supremacy of the constitution in the national legal order. third: the constitutional court may examine the ultra vires condition, that is to say, whether the actions of the union institutions infringe the principle of conferral, when the union institutions, bodies, offices and agencies have exceeded the limits of their competences in a way that infringes this principle. as a result of such a decision, ultra vires acts do not apply in the territory of a member state. four: the constitution prohibits delegation of powers to the extent that it would mean that the state could not be considered a sovereign and democratic country. i'll skip a few more quotes to save you a lot of time, but i'll just go over the last two. the constitution is the supreme law of poland in relation to all international agreements binding on it, including agreements on the transfer of competence in certain matters, the constitution shall have priority in its validity and application in the territory of poland. and last quote: the delegation of powers to the union must not violate the principle of the primacy of the constitution and must not violate any provision of the constitution. i can see the emotion on your faces. i understand that you disagree with that at least in part in this room. i just don't understand why, because these quotes refer to decisions of the french constitutional council, the danish supreme court, the german federal constitutional court. i have omitted the quotes from the italian, spanish courts, and the quotes from the polish court rulings relate to 2005 and 2010, so after poland became a member of the european union. and this doctrine that we defend today has been entrenched for years. professor marc safian, former president-in-office of the council. – mr president, madam commissioner, honourable members, the european council has recalled several times the european union’s goal of reinforcing resilience and facilitating the green transition. by putting forward a green deal in line with the objectives set out in the paris agreement, the european union committed to making europe the world’s first climate neutral continent by 2050. in order to achieve that, it is necessary to adjust and update our regulatory framework. therefore, the reform of state aid rules in the field of climate, energy and the environment is necessary in order to enable member states to support projects that contribute to achieving climate neutrality. the council therefore welcomes the work that the commission is currently undertaking in updating state aid guidelines and is looking forward to the adoption of new rules, scheduled by the end of the year. besides empowering member states to reach the goals of the green deal and allow governments to fund, when necessary, a larger share of the cost than before, the updated guidelines will focus on new flagship areas such as biodiversity, clean mobile infrastructure and research efficiency. the reform needs to take into account the importance of balance between supporting competitiveness and growth, maintaining a level playing field in the market, achieving the eu green ambitions and the ability to adapt to the individual situation in each member state. the new rules will also have to expand the scope of the general block exemption regulation, creating new ways for governments to invest in green infrastructure without requiring the commission’s approval in advance. the council will continue to support progress towards the long—term goal of climate neutrality, as appropriate.
executive vice-president of the commission. – mr president, honourable members, thank you for this opportunity to discuss the draft climate, energy and environmental protection state aid guidelines. of course, soon to be known by their abbreviation, so that we can keep it between us. now, i hope we can enable knowledge about the opportunities that the new guidelines will provide. from the simple fact that the green deal is our top priority, we need to fight climate change and we need to get the necessary resources to do so. the targets have been set. proposals have been tabled, in front of you. and the green deal is also our growth strategy. so that we can transform europe into a fair and prosperous society with a modern, resource-efficient and competitive economy. we want the transition to be just and to equip our industries with the tools to play their part in the transition. the recent spike in energy prices has demonstrated the urgency of this transition and the need to move away from fossil fuel dependency. reaching our ambitious targets involves nothing less than a transformation of the way that we power our lives. we have to make huge investments in infrastructure, in wind, in solar plants, in energy-efficient buildings, in networks that secure green mobility and in decarbonising industry. the magnitude of this investment challenge, requires mobilising both private and public funds in a way that ensures best value for money and crowds in private investment. the revision of our existing guidelines for energy and environment protection state aid will play a key role in helping member states provide adequate support to reach green deal objectives, where the markets cannot deliver alone. the new set of guidelines will provide a flexible, and we also hope, future—proof enabling framework to accompany the green deal. to that end, a number of examples as to what we do. we are proposing to broaden the scope of the guideline to facilitate support in new areas important for the green transition. this includes clean mobility, circularity, biodiversity and energy efficiency in buildings. our new guidelines would cover all technologies that can deliver the green deal, such as those for production of renewable and low-carbon hydrogen. renewable energy remains as important as ever in achieving our targets. member states continue to set up separate renewable schemes as they do today under a new, cross-cutting section on decarbonising measures. the flexibility also extends to the type of aid instruments and to the amount of aid. the draft guidelines accommodate calls by the industry to allow contracts for difference and also foresees that support may cover up to a 100% of the extra costs of greener investment – what we call the funding gap, where aid awards are based on competitive bidding. as a counterbalance to the increased flexibility, obviously we need safeguards to ensure that the aid is effectively directed to where it’s necessary to improve climate and environmental protection and is limited to what is necessary to achieve the environmental goals. those safeguards include public consultation above certain thresholds and open tenders being the general rule in most areas to ensure best value for taxpayers’ money. energy communities, they play an important role in ensuring citizen participation and, of course, also public acceptance. in line with the current case practice, it remains possible for member states to introduce specific features in their auctions to facilitate the participation of such communities in tenders, also where the thresholds for no tendering are exceeded. last but not least, we want our guidelines to work seamlessly together with and support relevant european legislation and policies in the environmental and energy field, and that also requires a coherent approach to ending subsidies for fossil fuels and particularly those which are most polluting. for those fossil fuels, the draft guidelines foresee that a positive assessment under state aid rules is unlikely in the light of the negative effects on the environment. in the same vein, we also need to avoid that support for gas in a transitional period creates lock-in effects, not compatible with the 2030 and 2050 climate targets. i would like to conclude with a few words on the process ahead of us. as you are most certainly aware, we launched a public consultation on the perpetuation of the guidelines that ended on 2 august. we received an impressive amount of contribution, more than 700, which also demonstrates the importance stakeholders and authorities attach to these guidelines. i want to say thank you for the valuable inputs and contributions also received from members of this parliament. in addition, meeting with member states took place in mid-july to collect feedback, to answer questions on the draft guidelines. in order to ensure legal certainty, our plan is still to adapt the revised guidelines by the end of the year. as you can hear, this debate is very, very well timed. in parallel, we are also undertaking a targeted revision of the general block exemption regulation. that regulation covers a wide range of state aid measures, which can be implemented without notification to the commission. we want that simplification to also be extended to investment in new technologies, such as renewable and low-carbon hydrogen and carbon capture and storage or use, and to areas that are key to achieve the objectives of the green deal; could be zero pollution, resource efficiency, biodiversity. ley provisions on clean mobility and energy performance of buildings were already introduced in july this year. in addition, the rules will be made more flexible with regard to the definition of eligible costs and aid intensities. a public consultation on the targeted revision of the block exemption regulation was launched at the beginning of this month and will run until 8 september. i am really happy that we can have this debate. as you can hear, it is really well timed and i’ll be looking forward to hearing your views.

with the high energy prices, i think that it is also important to note that the higher the gas prices, the higher the cost—effectiveness of the measures to mitigate methane emissions is, because methane should be used as a natural product rather than escaping to the atmosphere. on the international side, the international methane emissions observatory (imeo) will provide reliable data on methane emissions and will therefore represent a powerful tool to drive global action to reduce global methane emissions. the global methane pledge, as a joint eu—us initiative, represents a strong outcome of our renewed transatlantic agenda to continue and strengthen our cooperation on climate change and decarbonisation of energy. it includes a commitment to move towards using the best available inventory methodologies to quantify methane emissions, with a particular focus on high emission sources. as concerns the environmental legislation, we are reviewing the industrial emissions directive, the sewage sludge directive, the urban waste water treatment directive and the landfill directive. although it is too early to go into more details, i hope that, during the review process, and specific thematic focus groups of the european innovation partnership on methane emission reduction and carbon sequestration in grasslands. the eu soil strategy also has the potential to become a milestone in eu policies related to a healthy environment in the long run. the legislative ecosystem represented by the green deal will, directly and indirectly, affect millions of lives and jobs in all sectors, and the commission is particularly careful to ensure a fair and just green transition for all, especially vulnerable groups in the energy, agri—food and other sectors. in the post-2020 cap, member states will have the possibility to design a specific combination of interventions, reducing emissions from agriculture. still, rural development programmes will be the main tool for strategic plans for the cap. thank you for bringing to my attention many important issues concerning the reduction of methane emissions in your interventions today and, of course, in the report. i am rapporteur. – madam president, i would like to thank all colleagues for their comments and say frankly that i was trying to take into account their concerns, especially when they were based on scientific evidence. i have to try to do my best in this long process. following the recent climate agreement with the us, it is our best hope in the eu to be able to lead the world in the right direction. it is now the time to suggest and negotiate a binding global agreement on methane mitigation at the cop26 meeting in glasgow in line with the model pathways that limit global warming to 1.5°c from the intergovernmental panel on climate change (ipcc) special report, the ipcc sixth assessment report and the 2021 united nations environment programme (unep) global methane assessment. in this regard, it is of paramount importance to proceed with immediate and rapid reductions in methane emissions, paying attention to economic and social sustainability and, in this decade, it is one of the effective measures for the eu climate action. methane emission reduction complements the necessary reductions in carbon dioxide emissions and many of the emission cuts required by the paris agreement and could already be achieved with low cost, as the commission said, and technically feasible methane mitigation. commissioner, we fully endorse your approach and your arguments on methane reduction in the energy sector and we are looking forward to our cooperation. when it comes to the agriculture sector, i would like just to repeat that it is included in the report as it is important to establish a framework which incentivises and rewards farmers along with the entire value chain and especially frontrunners for their effort. i would like to kindly ask all of you, dear colleagues, here in this house on this day, to vote in favour and to support the eu strategy to reduce methane emission. now we should not think about the next election, but above all, about the next generation.

in writing. agriculture is cited as the main source of methane emissions in the eu (53%), followed by the waste sector (26%) and energy (19%). at the same time, we have to take into account the different effects on the atmosphere of biogenic methane from ruminants and methane from fossil fuels, and we have to assess them differently. in addition, we must not forget that agriculture holds enormous potential for reducing harmful emissions through investments in innovation, new feed additives, improved breeding and genetics, grazing, integrated manure management, production of biogas from agricultural waste, etc. in this respect, agriculture is part of the solution and good livestock management practices can lead to a 30% reduction in greenhouse gas emissions. to do that, we need to work with farmers, not against them, to reduce meat consumption and reduce animal husbandry. this production is vital for the preservation of rural communities and is an important source of employment in rural areas. farmers should have the necessary tools and financial incentives to implement carbon and methane capture practices in order to further reduce emissions in agriculture.
in writing. the european union's target of reducing all greenhouse gas emissions by 2030 includes methane emissions. methane is the second most important cause of climate change, after carbon dioxide. in this fight, the eu needs partners. without global efforts and international cooperation, this battle is already lost, as a significant part of global methane emissions comes from outside the eu. increased methane emissions affect biodiversity and agricultural production, while reducing methane emissions, together with the use of existing technologies, can provide multiple benefits, including better crop yields. the eu can limit emissions from agriculture through technological innovation, as well as incentives and partnerships with farmers. without financial incentives, european farmers will not be able to cope with the new european conditionalities and policies, and food security may be put at risk. the eu must ensure a level playing field for european producers and imports from third countries must meet the same standards. it is imperative to ensure a fair transition for all sectors where reductions in methane emissions can have a socio-economic impact, so as to avoid the relocation of economic and agricultural activities outside the european union.
the next item is the statement by the council and the commission on the first anniversary of the effective abolition of abortion in poland (2021/2925 ((rsp)).
president-in-office of the council. – madam president, abortion and reproductive rights are a highly sensitive and complex issue across europe, from both ethical and legal perspectives. they touch upon some of the most fundamental questions. the european council of human rights consistently ruled that member states enjoy a wide margin of appreciation as to whether, and under what circumstances, abortion is permitted under their national law. as far as the european union is concerned, primary law confirms that union law does not interfere with constitutional provisions and other national legislation of the member state relating to abortion. in accordance with article 168(7) of the treaty on the functioning of the european union, union action in the field of public health should respect the responsibilities of member states for the definition of their health policy and for the organisation and delivery of health services and medical care. in this context, the european pillar of social rights states that everyone has the right to timely access to affordable, preventive and corrective health care of good quality.
member of the commission. – madam president, one year ago, the ruling of the polish constitutional court on abortion, resulting in a near—total ban on abortion, sparked a wave of protests in poland. the eu has no competence on abortion rights within a member state. legislation in this area is up to the member state concerned. when making use of their competences, member states must respect fundamental rights, which bind them by virtue of their national constitutions and commitments under international law. the european court of human rights has recognised the lack of access to abortion services as a violation of the right to family and private life. all women across the eu should have equal access to good quality healthcare and treatment. sexual and reproductive health is integral to our general health. we hear of situations in poland, such as unsafe underground abortions, women with financial means going abroad to have abortions, but without medical follow up at home, and even more difficult situations arising for women in a vulnerable position. the covid—19 pandemic has made the reality even more challenging. women’s rights are a gauge for the overall situation of fundamental rights. high-quality sexual and reproductive health services are essential to women and girls, as well as for men and boys. while often any reference to sexual and reproductive health and rights is quickly linked to abortion, they also cover issues such as contraception, education, prevention, treatment of hiv and other sexually transmitted diseases, as well as fertility and sex-specific cancers. these rights are core to gender equality. the commission continues to monitor the developments in all member states regarding gender equality. we encourage member states to safeguard women’s equal access to good quality healthcare services.

for the left. mr president, madam rapporteur, ladies and gentlemen, i am very pleased that we have succeeded today in concluding the work on the directive on motor vehicle liability insurance, and i would like to thank the rapporteur, mrs ditta charanz, for her work in removing the controversial requirement for compulsory cover for electric bicycles, scooters and garden tractors from the commission's proposal. that would be a step in the wrong direction and would certainly not help the reputation of the european union. some motor vehicles, such as electric bicycles and segways, are smaller in size and therefore less likely than other vehicles to cause significant damage to health or property. moreover, this measure would also have a significant impact on older citizens who have no money to spare. vehicles intended exclusively for motor sports are also excluded from the scope of the directive, as these vehicles are usually covered by other types of liability insurance and are not covered by compulsory motor insurance if they are used only for competition purposes. in two years' time, it will also be much easier to negotiate a mandatory guarantee for cars registered in another member state. motor insurance also has a significant impact on the free movement of persons, goods and vehicles and thus on the internal market and the schengen area. i believe that this directive will create legal certainty and harmonise what should be covered by insurance. motorists no longer have to worry about different rules between member states. the negative impacts on a wide range of stakeholders, including injured parties, insurers, guarantee funds and motor vehicle insurers, resulting from the legal disparity will be eliminated. i think we have all done a good job, and i thank you very much for it, because it will be of benefit to the citizens of the european union in particular.

vice-president of the commission / high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, thank you very much for this lively debate on a lively reality. we have used the concept of 'hybrid war' a lot - and i have used it myself - and if you refer to the definitions we normally use to make sense of the words, a hybrid war is a process that combines destabilisation operations - not necessarily violent - with a battle of information or disinformation and that can also generate violent situations or military actions as a consequence of the tension created by the destabilisation processes. that said, what is happening on the border of belarus certainly deserves to be called that because it fits the definition, but i think we should make an effort to avoid an escalation of war terms, we should avoid increasing tension by using tense words: i do not think that the war or neo-war climate we are creating with the discourse of wars, raids, etc. will help us much in having a full knowledge of what is happening in order to give a constructive response. yes, we can use the terms in the sense that the technical literature gives them, but we should also avoid embarking on a dynamic where the terms 'war', 'invasion' etc. would not serve the purpose that we have, which is at this moment to protect the borders of the union, without a doubt; to deal with a humanitarian crisis, too, and to respect our laws and our procedures, also in this case, and the schengen code, which is intended for all kinds of situations. so, ladies and gentlemen, what is clear is that we are dealing with the exploitation of people to be used as instruments of pressure against our borders. call it what you will, but we are witnessing a massive disinformation operation - i see here my colleague the commissioner responsible for fighting it - a massive disinformation operation in many countries at once, where people are told that there is a way to the promised land; the promised land is us, europe, which for many people is the hope for a better life. and the scenes and information we have from the intelligence services that we share with the member states clearly show that this operation is very orchestrated, that at the beginning it was only one flight a week from baghdad and now - i will give an example of an airline linked to an oligarch cousin of bashar al-assad who until now was engaged in transporting the troops of the wagner group and who has now found an apparently more lucrative activity, that in one week has made twenty rotations between damascus and belarus and has sold all its tickets for the next flights. it is an absolutely measured operation based on deception, and this deception is producing huge profits for many people: there are belarusian consuls who have travel agencies; on friday morning they are consuls and in the afternoon they sell tickets. a lot of people are making a lot of money, and we certainly have to cut this flow: we got that with iraq and we're trying to do that now. our colleague, vice-president schinas, will be visiting the transit countries, which are not all countries of origin, but increasingly are no longer iraqis: they are syrians, they are afghans, they are all those who have found temporary refuge in some transit country and now believe that they can reach europe and end up between two walls; the walls may not be walls, but they are obstacles: a closed border and belarusian guards who, once they have brought them to it, prevent them from going back. firstly, we must respect our schengen codes, and our schengen codes say that there must be border crossing points where people can be checked, and that the principle of non-refoulement must be respected, and that certainly we must monitor illegal border crossing, but there must be checkpoints. we must combine the defence of our border - our border, and i say this in the plural, because the border of poland, lithuania and latvia is a european border - with respect for our laws and regulations and we must do everything we can to prevent a humanitarian crisis arising at the very foot of europe, the pole of our border. and for that, and many have asked me to do that, and believe me, we will do everything we can to get it done, the aid agencies need to be able to help these people and be able to get to them from both sides: we haven't got it yet, but i hope we can get it done. secondly, we must raise the tone of the political debate and take the issue to the united nations: this is no longer a matter of bilateral dialogue between us and belarus, we are witnessing a massive operation of human rights violation that deserves to be discussed in the highest international political body, which is the united nations, and i intend to use the diplomatic means that we and the member states have to raise the issue at the highest level. and of course we have to continue to fight the lukashenka regime, but it will not fall tomorrow, and the day after tomorrow we may find people who are not able to survive in the circumstances in which they have found themselves as a result of the deception they have suffered and the lack of respect for their dignity from the belarusian regime. we have to do all that. i appreciate your opinions, your criticisms, your different points of view, but i believe that europe must be united in this; united around things which must not be incompatible with each other: united around the defence of our border, our territory; united around respect for our values, which are based on laws, and united in the ways and methods we have to prevent this flow from continuing and that those who have come this far have a way of returning. someone asked, "back where?" going back to where they came from for a lot of them. because if they cannot all enter europe, what is certain is that they cannot stay at the foot of our border forever. thank you for your support, thank you for this discussion: it is a good opportunity to show what europe stands for in the world.

i have to say that i am not in favour of this. the commission is therefore proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the following areas: a critical blog post, a harsh tweet, an open letter to the government, the publication of articles after intensive research. all of this sounds like harmless activities that are done millions of times a day. however, all these simple actions can have dramatic consequences. more and more journalists, ngos and activists are facing lawsuits, simply because they are exposing public criticism of scandals. these lawsuits are not about legally defending themselves, but powerful individuals and organizations are pursuing strategic lawsuits to get rid of critics. our courts, which were created to protect legitimate interests, are increasingly being abused by these same powerful individuals and organizations. and these strategic lawsuits against public participation are a slap in the face to the defendants and are therefore also called slapp lawsuits. i'm not talking about a few slapp lawsuits. slapp actions are becoming more and more common in the european union. the swedish media company realtid media has been repeatedly threatened with lawsuits as a result of its reporting. the polish activists of the atlas of hate are currently being sued by several governments. in the german state of hesse, initiatives promoting democracy and opposing right-wing extremism are increasingly facing lawsuits. what do all these cases have in common? first, victims of slapp lawsuits are simply doing their jobs. second, the plaintiffs have no intention of defeating the defendants. it's not about winning. the procedure is only instituted to force the victims into expensive, complicated, lengthy and nerve-wracking procedures. at the same time, it is intended to deter other critics. but not only that, slapp lawsuits have an impact not only on the victims but also on their families. daphne caruana galizia was facing 47 lawsuits at the time of her murder, and her children are still facing the same lawsuits as legal successors. all these examples show that we in the eu need to act urgently. no one, really no one, should be silenced by strategic lawsuits. those who make public criticism, who publish research, must be able to be sure that they will not be subject to reprisals, intimidation and threats. democracy thrives on the discourse of different opinions. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. we have the backing of numerous civil society organisations, academics, judges, lawyers and victims of slapp lawsuits to make our eu-wide consistent proposals. we want measures of a legal nature. this includes a review of the applicable international rules of private law in order to avoid complaint tourism. we want a binding directive with minimum standards to protect against slapp lawsuits with an eu-wide definition. at the same time, we need complementary non-legislative measures, such as a fund to support victims of slapp cases, so that legal costs can be covered or psychological support can be organised. of course, we need to actively train judges and lawyers to recognize slapp lawsuits. because despite the enormous number of complaints, the phenomenon is not yet sufficiently perceived. so instead of intimidating those who point out wrongdoing, we should be backing them up. it is not the victims of slapp who should be brought to justice, but those who abuse our legal system who should be held accountable for their intimidation, and that is why we need this initiative.
rapporteur. – mr president, tiemo and myself, as co-rapporteurs, come from different committees and different political families, and we have come together for a shared purpose, presenting this cross-party, cross-committee report in plenary today in what i consider to be a very important moment. important for our institution, that meps came together to adopt a report that protects journalists. important for our european democracy that this report is not only adopted but also implemented. important for our societies’ gatekeepers that they know that we have their backs when they have nowhere else to turn to. strategic lawsuits against public participation (slapps) are lawsuits that seek to muzzle our journalists and provide a chilling effect on public participation. they do this by financially and emotionally draining their targets, starting out with threats and continuing with legal action. trends have shown an increase of these kinds of lawsuits over the past years. we need to be clear: this is not about people not being able to protect their reputation, this is about the abuse of our legal systems, and there is a fine balance that we have managed to achieve in this report. the slapp strategy is simple but effective, with criminals literally shopping around our jurisdictions, scouting out favourable laws to serve their purposes. in effect, this means that individual journalists are faced with a number of lawsuits filed against them in foreign jurisdictions. at that point, journalists are faced with a choice: stop reporting the facts or face costly and lengthy lawsuits in another foreign country. so journalists lose the case before it even starts. in some member states, lawsuits are filed against them in their personal capacity in legal systems they are unaware of and have no connection with, meaning that, if they leave their job with a media house, the case could still follow them around. mounting a defence is practically impossible, so those with the means get what they want and the story is effectively killed. our message is: this is unacceptable. these lawsuits do not seek to obtain a favourable outcome, but they seek to intimidate. we have a system today that favours those who seek to hide the truth over those who seek to expose it. so there is no equality of arms in the system. there is no justice in the system, and we in this parliament want to change that. this european parliament has long been at the forefront of calling for a new anti-slapp legislation, and we want this report to be the foundation of a new eu anti-slapp directive. we have made sure that we have as many safeguards as necessary to protect our press, our journalists and civil society from slapps while remaining within what is possible under the eu treaties. we are calling for a reform of the brussels 1a regulation to prevent forum shopping, and calling for the introduction of a uniform choice of law rule for defamation and the rome 2 regulation to give legal certainty. what we want do is combine legislation with complementary measures and create a system where judges are able to take a quick a priori decision that would see obviously vexatious lawsuits dismissed quickly and this means investing in training and creating systems that would allow for this. our report calls for a fund, as said by my colleague, for slapp victims, for legal fees, legal aid, psychological support, training and an online information and support hub for potential victims of slapps. we can make a difference. we look forward to listening to you, colleagues, the shadow rapporteurs we have worked excellently with, and also to you, commissioner, we look forward to hearing from you.
vice-president of the commission. – mr president, honourable members, i am pleased to join you in view of the adoption of the european parliament’s own-initiative report to address the phenomenon of strategic lawsuits against public participation (slapp). i wish to congratulate the co-rapporteurs, roberta metsola and tiemo wölken, for their excellent work. four years have passed since the tragic assassination of daphne caruana galizia and already, as we heard from mr wölken, at the time of her death, daphne had a shocking number of 47 slapp cases pending, and many are still, even now, fought by her family. abusive litigation against those whose job it is to inform our citizens on issues of public interest seems to be gaining ground in the european union. there is growing evidence that, in particular, journalists and rights defenders are targets of this and our rule of law report of 2021 includes details on that. together with increasing threats to their physical and online safety, legal threats and abusive litigation add to an environment where hostile activity against journalists is growing and can have a serious impact on their willingness and ability to continue their work. their work, as well as that of rights defenders, is fundamental for the health of our democracies and for the rule of law. our democracies depend on the active engagement of journalists and civil society speaking up when the public interest is at stake. together, we are making progress towards the eu initiative announced by the commission to protect journalists and rights defenders against abusive lawsuits. allow me to expand on the commission’s plans in this regard. after mapping and assessing the situation in the member states, we believe that the most efficient way to fight against slapp and prevent it from growing roots in the eu would be a solid and balanced combination of legislative and non-legislative measures. parliament’s own-initiative report also calls for such a combination in order to address as many angles as possible of this complex phenomenon. the legislative action that we aim to propose would be targeted legislation that will lay out procedural safeguards against slapp in cross-border civil proceedings. the proposal will need to ensure a careful balance of fundamental rights, freedom of speech and freedom of expression on the one hand, and access to justice for all, on the other hand. the legislative action would be complemented by non-legislative measures covering aspects such as raising awareness about slapp, training for judges and potential targets, support and monitoring of slapp cases. we are also considering recommendations to the member states to adopt legislation in the same direction as the legislation we planned for cross-border cases. our aim is to ensure the most efficient combination of measures we can envisage, while respecting subsidiarity and proportionality. i consider that such a package would best serve the purpose. the preparatory work is well under way, including the launch of a public consultation, which is ongoing. i also had a discussion with the justice ministers on 7 october, and we are pursuing both technical interactions and bilateral talks to explain our initiative. as a next step, we will organise a stakeholders’ meeting on 25 november, at which the two rapporteurs have kindly agreed to present the main findings of the european parliament report, for which i would like to thank you again, and i look forward to our discussion. finally, let me stress that the anti-slapp initiative will be reinforced by other actions to ensure a proper working environment for journalists and safeguarding media freedom and pluralism. this is in particular through the recently adopted recommendation on the safety of journalists and the upcoming action on a new european media freedom act. we need to act with determination and by tackling several angles so as to safeguard the democratic space, and i know i can count on your continued support in this regard.

in writing. in this debate, we are discussing the report on strengthening democracy and media freedom and pluralism in the eu in the light of the misuse of civil and criminal proceedings to silence journalists, ngos and civil society. unfortunately, there are practices that are aimed at intimidating or even forcing individual journalists or activists to stop publishing or acting. the main issue is slapp, or 'strategic lawsuits against public participation'. these are usually brought by influential individuals, companies or public authorities against journalists or activists. they may be designed to deter actors from acting or publishing for fear of legal costs or time-consuming proceedings, even if the court would ultimately rule against the party bringing the action. these are not hypothetical mechanisms: the murdered maltese investigative journalist daphne caruana galizia had 47 court cases against her at the time of her death. i believe that journalists should be protected and their private and family life should not be violated. but remember that not everything can or should be regulated at eu level. freedom of speech and the right to express one's views are fundamental rights that are guaranteed by eu law. these issues should be regulated at member state level.

member of the commission. mr president, honourable members of parliament, first of all i would like to thank you very much for this report on the establishment of a european strategy for critical raw materials. i would like to begin by thanking the rapporteur, hildegard bentele, very much for this extremely important work - thank you very much, hildegard - and, of course, the fictitious rapporteurs, but also the members of the various committees who contributed to this work. you have said it, but i would like to repeat it in my own words, if i may: access to raw materials is really at the heart of our industrial policy. the pandemic has revealed this even more than before. now, with the recovery, of course, we realize that the resilience of our value chains within the internal market itself, but also in terms of the green transition and the digital transition, is clearly dependent on our ability to ensure the security of supply of the essential value chains. the conclusion is simple and the same everywhere: europe has allowed a strong dependence on sources of supply in third countries to develop - perhaps too strong. rare earths, magnesium, lithium, graphite are obviously all the necessary components for everything that makes up our green transition and our digital transition -- batteries, but also all the critical components that we're going to talk about a lot in the years and decades to come. but our raw material needs will obviously increase considerably. for example, we're going to need 60 times more lithium and 15 times more cobalt by 2050 for electric batteries alone, and 10 times more rare earths. this, of course, without mentioning the raw material requirements for all industrial applications that will accompany the digital transition, especially in semiconductors, but not only. we have seen how geopolitics, what i call the geopolitics of value chains, is at work for our systemic partners or rivals. i say the geopolitics of value chains because that is what it is all about. our dependencies have become geostrategic instruments which are often used against us and our interests. and that can have serious consequences. we are seeing it, for example, in semiconductors, in terms of our ability to produce, or even to recover from the crisis we have been through and are still going through. this is particularly true, of course, for the whole of access to critical raw materials. this is why, just over a year ago, you will recall, in september 2020, the commission adopted an action plan on critical raw materials. your report clearly shows the alignment, if i may say so, of our two institutions in the analysis of the situation. so we are very much in sync, if i may say so, and we are converging on the need to build our resilience in strategic value chains. this work is based on three pillars. first, diversifying our sources of supply. strategic partnerships have already been established with some countries, such unbiased. whether it is our partners or our competitors, we must of course do so, and i repeat this in this house, without naivety: we must anticipate and counter any attempt to use access to raw materials as a means of geopolitical pressure on the union and its businesses - what can be called hybrid threats and which we see in other areas, alas! the second point i would like to highlight in this report concerns the circular economy. it is a pillar of our joint work, not only for the purpose of 'greening', if i may say so, but also to improve security of supply and, therefore, obviously, to reduce our strategic dependencies. we have proposed this, for example, in our proposal for the battery regulation, by aiming for higher recycling rates, in particular for lithium, cobalt, graphite or nickel. a similar approach could be used for other critical raw materials, such as rare earths, which you mentioned earlier, madam rapporteur, and also in areas where production is almost exclusively concentrated, so to speak, outside the union. we also agreed that recycling of critical raw materials, while essential, will not be enough on its own to meet the increased demand for these in writing. the european parliament must take the side of farmers. it took months of hard negotiations for us to be able to debate today the next seven years of the common agricultural policy. a lot of people in this house, for a long time, didn't get the gist of this debate. and that is that european farmers are the ones who put good quality and safe food on our table. therefore, if we impose unrealistic environmental requirements on them, we endanger the food supply of european citizens. it took the agricultural ministers of the member states to take a firm stand before a compromise proposal was finally put forward. a proposal that strikes a balance between supporting farming and protecting nature. we are living in a time of crisis that we could not have imagined before. the reason why quality food is still on store shelves is that we can always count on farmers. but today, they're counting on us! let's send them a clear message, then. i ask you all to support the proposal for a common agricultural policy.
in writing. the common agricultural policy is one of the key eu policies. it is directly applicable in all member states. it carries out tasks of a social and economic dimension, but also purely political ones. this is evidenced by the wide range of cap objectives. increasing the productivity of european agriculture, supporting technical progress in rural areas, developing production and stabilising agricultural markets are just some of them. the cap also plays an important role in ensuring an adequate standard of living for rural people by supporting farmers' incomes. it is also an important element of the union's internal market, since it is designed to ensure that, in addition to stabilising national markets, agricultural products are reasonably priced for all consumers. over the decades of its existence, the cap has been reformed on several occasions. now, with the entry into force of the new eu multiannual budget, it is time for another review. the union and the member states are facing new environmental and climate challenges. i believe that among the many changes planned for the cap after 2023, changes are needed in the definition of agricultural activity so that subsidies go to people actually engaged in agricultural production and not to owners of latifundia aimed only at receiving eu subsidies. increased support for small farms and young farmers, as well as greater transparency and compliance of the reform with labour law. in this context, the european parliament should give its unambiguous support to the adoption of a package of regulations reforming the common agricultural policy.
in writing. the common agricultural policy plays a key role in the union budget and is of great importance to countries such as lithuania, where agriculture is a significant sector of the economy. the cap offers direct payments and funds to farmers under the second pillar, which is a major help not only for food security but also for investment and employment in rural areas. the cap cuts are unacceptable. for this reason, the cap should focus on core areas of activity and the cap allocation for the eu-27 for the period 2021-2027 should remain at least at the level of the 2014-2020 budget, while providing for a starting amount for the reserve in case of crises in the agricultural sector. the continuing discrimination against farmers in the so-called new member states on the basis of unequal payments must also be stopped. harmonisation of the levels of direct payments in the member states is essential to ensure a level playing field in the single internal market. there is an urgent need for a fair distribution of direct payments between member states. the new cap must also include tailor-made measures to help farmers overcome crises and more support for small farms and young farmers. these should be the main priorities of the future cap.

purposes. these people are trapped on belarusian territory because of the recklessness of the lukashenko regime, and these people need help. this is why we immediately got in touch with the un agencies, the international organization for migration (iom) and the united nations high commissioner for refugees (unhcr). we have set up a contact group with them, we are in constant contact and we immediately mobilized funding to support their efforts on the ground. second, on our diplomatic outreach, here too i discussed with president biden to align our efforts. we agreed that, to counter this behaviour, it is important to coordinate our sanctions and to work with the countries of origin and with the airlines that are transporting migrants to minsk. that is what we have done and that is what we are doing. we are in the process of coordinating our sanctions with the united states, canada and the united kingdom. i immediately tasked vice president schinas to engage with the key countries. he's been to iraq, the united arab emirates, lebanon and turkey, and he's going to uzbekistan soon. high representative and vice-president borrell convened the foreign affairs council to expand the sanctions regime, and commissioner johansson was in egypt. i would like to thank all three of them for their successful and tireless work. we can already see the impact on the ground. we see that several airlines and civil aviation authorities have stopped unwarranted travel to belarus. furthermore, iraq has begun repatriating nationals stranded in belarus. we very much welcome this very good cooperation with iraq. but more migrants are trapped, and we will work with the un agencies to facilitate their return home. we will mobilise up to eur 3.5 million to support voluntary returns to belarus, and our efforts and this outreach will continue. mon troisième point porte sur les sanctions. i would like to thank the commissioner for his reply. the strategy of belarus is based very concretely on the complicity of the tour operators and their intermediaries. there are indeed specialist travel agencies offering all-inclusive services: visas, flights, hotels and, in a rather cynical manner, taxis and buses up to the border. we are very clear: these migrants are being deceived by infamous false promises. we must really fight against this and that is why we propose to establish a blacklist for all means and modes of transport, on the basis of international legislation on the trafficking and smuggling of migrants. the commission is today presenting a legislative proposal to that effect. this proposal should be adopted in codecision, so i say to the members that i am counting on your swift action to adopt it as soon as possible. fourth and last point: the management of frontiers. our position has always been to support our member states in the front line, both in the east and in the south. the european union is the only institution in the world which is able to do so. we are currently deploying important efforts. in the new european budget, €6.4 billion is available for border management. we finance equipment such as electronic surveillance technologies, patrol vehicles, equipment for border guards and the construction of border crossing points, but also satellite images and critical infrastructure. it is the management of the frontiers that we support. in addition, we spend about €1 billion per year for frontex and, today, the college has decided to do even more. we propose to triple the funds currently allocated to lithuania, latvia and poland. this package of security measures must make it possible to cope with the current emergency and underline our solidarity with the member states situated on the front line. member states facing such a hybrid attack must be able to respond effectively to the emergency situation they face. at the same time, they need to fully respect fundamental rights and international obligations. both points are crucial and we need to find a way to reconcile them. we are therefore working on a proposal for provisional emergency measures in the area of asylum and return, based on article 78 (3) of the treaty. the aim is to support member states to set up the right processes to manage irregular arrivals in a swift and orderly way, in line with fundamental rights. last, but not least, what is happening at the border with belarus belongs to a broader context. recent actions by the lukashenko regime and its supporters are a determined attempt to create a continuing and protracted crisis. let me repeat: the european union does not recognise this regime, which violently represses its own people. these actions are part of a concerted effort to destabilize the european union and our neighborhood. this includes ukraine and moldova in particular. these actions represent a real and present danger to our union's security. these actions go beyond belarus. they are testing our resolve and unity. but the european union has the will, the unity and the resolve to face this and future crises, and with your support, honourable members, we will stand the test. this is why today, more than ever, i say long live europe.
